#3823. WoW: Forever ultimate impressions—Vanilla Plus approach makes Classic an exciting adventure once more

This month, I had the amazing opportunity to join all of you in the WoW: Forever beta and see all the new and exciting features Blizzard introduced into the Vanilla experience to make it fresh and intriguing for everyone, not just the old heads who were around in 2004. I absolutely loved what I saw, even though some archaic Vanilla mechanics remain in place.

The Skyborne race was my faction of choice, aligned with the Alliance of course. I was a Rogue, like most of my characters in WoW, except in post-WOTLK expansions where I would pick anything, level it to 55, and then go and make a blood Death Knight.

This new race’s starting zone was refreshing. It had a plethora of different areas clearly drawing inspiration from other locations in Vanilla WoW, and moving from one place to another gave you a sense of progression through its environmental storytelling alone. It boasted a lot of cool ancient temples, alongside dark forests shrouded in mist and mystery and strange cities attuned to the very world and the powers of the wind.

The leveling in general was fine. The quests mostly followed the usual MMORPG formula of go there, kill that many creatures, and by chance loot them to bring me their unique items. That’s the overall gist, but some of the quests did have narrative grounding, and the writing in the quests themselves was actually better than I had expected of modern WoW. However, the structure of the zone meant a lot of players skipped most of its content and never saw the ultimate showdown, i.e., the zone’s narrative conclusion.

This is both good and bad. The game does not force you to stay in this zone for much longer than you want to, and as soon as you’re fed up and done, you can go to one of the ships and reach Dalaran, Stormwind, or any other faction capital you want to visit. Once there, you get quests that take you across the world and allow you to pick up leveling from areas in regular Vanilla WoW, but staying in the starting Skyborne zone is an option.

Read what’s behind the latest news in gaming (with a bit of snark) by subscribing to the Destructoid Checkpoint newsletter!

It starts to drag after level 10 or so, though, so leaving for Stormwind was actually what I did around level 13 and started my journey across the Eastern Kingdoms using boats and trains and walking on foot.

It was an adventure of sorts—I hadn’t played World of Warcraft for a long time now, and had not set foot in Vanilla for literally 15 years. This solemn odyssey across the world, to Teldrassil and the Ironforge and into Westfall and through Stormwind, was a trip down memory lane into a time that longer exists, a childhood I was born into, of which remain unseen fragments that only the mind’s eye can glimpse.

The overall experience, significantly boosted by the unprecedented amount of other players achieved both through nostalgia and the new no-realm system, was one that slingshot me back to the good old days, and I’m glad I got to play it.

I recommend checking WoW: Forever out if you liked old WoW but wanted something new added to the mix. The Vanilla is intact if you want to ignore all the novelties, but you always keep the option to try them out.

Nine years ago, Matt Filer officially began work on the OpenCAGE mod tools for Alien: Isolation—following two-and-a-half years of work on prototype versions. During that time the tools have been available for anyone to use, which is part of the reason Creative Assembly's legendarily scary horror game has a variety of mods already. (Though the VR mod works differently, since it's actually enabling an unfinished mode that shipped with the game.)

OpenCAGE has finally made it to version 1.0, which can be downloaded on Steam. Filer proudly told us his mod tools have "now reached the point where you're able to implement full custom maps, missions, modes, characters, weapons, animations, sounds, models, textures, and more!"

As a demonstration of what's possible, Filer is making a Halo-themed custom map. "It features custom cinematics, enemies, weapons, all on a brand new map with a custom HUD," he said. "It has reached a point now of being able to make full total conversion mods, which has always been my end goal, so it's cool to finally be here!"

Alien: Isolation just won our scariest videogame poll, and I consider it a well-earned victory. It's one of the few games I've seen frighten even people who aren't normally bothered by horror thanks to how unpredictable and relentless the xenomorph is when pursuing you. And those dead-eyed Worker Joe robots are no slouches either.

Hopefully some creative mods will give us reason to go back to Alien: Isolation, and help tide over the wait for the upcoming Alien: Isolation 2, which is likely to be available some time in 2027.

#3821. COD Modern Warfare 4's controversial Possum ability nerfed to stop it being used "as a combat mechanic instead of a survival mechanic"

Since the launch of Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4's DMZ mode, players have been mainly arguing about two topics: whether there's a need for a PvE-only mode, and whether Possum - an in-game trait - has a place in an extraction experience.

And developer Infinity Ward has clearly taken a side in the Possum argument by implementing a key change to how it works. In Modern Warfare 4's latest patch, released overnight, the developer made it so that Possum - an ability that can revive a player - cannot be activated while the team that killed you is nearby. Possum also can't be activated if it's been less than four minutes since you were killed.

These two should address the most common complaints, but Infinity Ward left space for further tweaks in the future, such as by adjusting its range and duration.

If you're unfamiliar, Possum allows a player to revive themselves from a completely dead state once per match. To other players around, you appear to be dead and your body can be looted. But by using Possum, clever players were able to exact immediate revenge on their killers - or anyone else standing around near their apparent corpse - by springing back to life and shooting them in the back.

Possum's intended use was for dead players to have another shot at extracting from the match, rather than forfeiting the run entirely. Though their loot may be lost, Possum allowed players to save their operator.

Infinity Ward underlined this intention in a note accompanying the change. "The intention for Possum is to give a high level operator a second chance," the developer said in a blog post. "With the current iteration, Possum was being used as a combat mechanic instead of a survival mechanic.

"These tweaks are meant to prevent players from getting right back into the fight which they had just lost. We will be watching the use of Possum with this change to see if it has the desired effect."

Outside of that DMZ change, the 28th October patch includes a round of weapon balance changes. There are several buffs to assault rifles and SMGs, and some nerfs to the APOC-338 and FiNN LMGs. The buffs are notable given the across-the-board nerf Infinity Ward experimented with during the second beta weekend for Modern Warfare 4, which sought to increase the time-to-kill (TTK) impact of weapons, making them feel weaker as a result.

The patch also fixes several bugs players have been able to exploit in multiplayer and DMZ. And, in case you missed it, this is the patch that adds the Shipment map to the game - and yes, there's a 24/7 playlist.

Eurogamer's full review of Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 is due later today.

J-Law airs out a couple of unexpected Oscar regrets.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Is Jennifer Lawrence ever going to live down that moment when she tripped right before winning her first Oscar? I’d blame the dress, even though I loved the moment and thought it was so real. That’s not what the actress is doing. She just talked about her iconic 2013 fashion moment at the Academy Awards, and it wasn’t the gown’s puffy quality that she’s doubtful about all these years later.

If you can believe it, it’s been over thirteen years since Lawrence accepted Best Actress for Silver Linings Playbook at the age of 22. These days she’s 36, more seasoned and a mother of two kids. Here’s some of her thoughts on the gown now:

It was a wedding dress. And, I think I was clearly looking at dresses going, ‘More, more, more!’ It’s a Dior Couture by Raf Simons. And it’s beautiful. You got to put your hair back if you’ve got a huge bottom… bottom of the dress. So I’m happy we went with, like, loose back.

J-Law could be ungrateful for the dress after the drama it caused her. I mean once she even had to defend why the fall wasn’t fake, and has recalled an even cringier moment that happened that night. Although it was still clearly a very special moment for her, and there’s a lot she still loves about what she wore over a decade later. You can see her talking about it here:

A post shared by The Talent Group (@thetalentgroup)

It really was a wonderful Oscar dress. Again, I’d think J-Law would be complaining about the volume of the lower half of the dress, but something else came up for her.

Honestly, I think it aged quite well. This is the one complaint she had about the dress:

I don’t know about the backwards necklace. Maybe those will come back. But look at her. She’s so tired and happy.

The “backlace” is definitely a style that’s come and gone over the years (as most trends go). It most famously was a thing back in the 1920s and 1930s, but has been revived again and again by Old Hollywood, then Princess Diana in the 80s and this J-Law moment was part of a more recent uptick in it.

While J-Law wasn’t sure about it now, the backlace was all the rage on red carpets in 2025. W Magazine noticed the trend on the likes of Margaret Qualley, Michelle Yeoh and Sabrina Carpenter. Regardless, here’s a couple more critiques the actress had to say about that momentous night:

Lift up the dress when you walk up the stairs. Remember to thank the director. I was too superstitious at the time to write a speech because I was like, ‘If I write it down, and prepare then I won’t win. And, I think I would just tell the 22-year-old, ‘That’s not true. And you’ll regret it.’ [Laughs].

Fair advice from her older self! While she might be a tad critical of that night, I think she had one of the most memorable and fabulous Oscars ever. Goodness knows what I would have done if I was televised at 22 years old in a massive dress. You can see Lawrence next in the new Hunger Games movie, Sunrise on the Reaping, out November 20.

Yoshida says the divisive expansion's sluggish pace "shows shortcomings on my part as the director," which seems a tad harsh

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Final Fantasy 14 producer and director Naoki "Yoshi-P" Yoshida knows one of Dawntrail's biggest issues at launch was the story's pacing, so the team is putting in the work to ensure that Evercold doesn't suffer the same fate.

Speaking to the media at Final Fantasy 14's Japanese leg of Fan Fest, Yoshida takes a question about what the team behind the MMO has learned from Dawntrail and how important it has been for Evercold's development.

"This time we are putting in serious consideration on the sense of tempo," Yoshida says, per a mod from the Final Fantasy 14 subreddit who was in attendance. "Back at Dawntrail we were being really careful in depicting new lands, new cultures, new encounters and this greatly slowed down the pacing on story progression. The fact that this did not align with players’ motivation of 'keep moving forward' shows shortcomings on my part as the director."

To remedy the pacing issues for Evercold, Yoshida says the team is moving some of the aforementioned focus to side quests, meaning you can enjoy that kind of thing if and when you want.

"This is actually connected to Final Fantasy 14's overall evolution, so we have to consider how precious players' time they have here," Yoshida adds. "After all, we will face the fact on how it's difficult for this to be relatable to players if the story doesn't progress at a brisk, fast-paced tempo, therefore we are placing a strong emphasis on this aspect this time."

I have been cautiously optimistic about Evercold since it was unveiled early this year, and this is another step in the right direction. While Dawntrail's story does eventually get good – doubly so in the post-expansion patches – it puts you in the position of having to defend it by telling your raid-brained pals to "stick with it, honestly," which is not an amazing place to be in games or other media like TV or film.

Dawntrail had other issues, sure, though Square Enix has shown enough consideration about that elsewhere. Of course, how this all works will remain to be seen. I've played Final Fantasy 14 for a long ol' time, and I've seen expansions launch with pacing issues – looking at you, Stormblood – that were remedied in later expansions. Hopefully Evercold sticks the landing in a way that hangs around for many expansions after.

#3817. World of Warcraft players angry after Blizzard seems to contradict housing cosmetics policy with Halloween additions

The World of Warcraft team has found itself at the centre of controversy after recently-added housing cosmetics appeared to go against previous pledges not to sell decorations tied to the visual identity of the game's races and factions.

The cosmetics are the haunted Grimtide Estate and Grimtide decor packs - a spooky spin on Kul Tiran furniture that players can either buy through the Battle.net store or in-game shop. These decorations have a nautical theme, in line with the buildings present in the Battle For Azeroth expansion, where the Kul Tiran subfaction was added for Alliance players.

This has drawn the ire of World of Warcraft fans because it appears to go against a 2025 developer blog by Blizzard, which stated: "Housing items tied to core fantasies of a player's race or class, or that already exist in Azeroth, won't be sold in the shop. Thematically important decor that players know and love will also not appear in the shop."

Many of the housing items shown off in the Grimtide cosmetics appear to be visually tied to the Kul Tiran subrace, and some are almost identical to furniture seen in the Battle for Azeroth expansion. For example, a Grimtide dining chair with an anchor decoration carved into its back rest would not look out of place at all in a Kul Tiran house.

The counter-argument, however, is that these are differentiated enough by being Halloween themed. For example, the Grimtide Grand Piano has a big green tentacle slithering out of the instrument, which perhaps makes it spooky enough, and distinct enough, to be considered d separate from regular Kul Tiran furniture.

But even if you accept that argument, these decorations undeniably come close to the red line Blizzard itself established. And it is not the first time Blizzard has come under fire for its microtransactions.The Burning Crusade Classic Deluxe Edition included a special mount that was a point of controversy from players stalwartly against the inclusion of microtransactions in the game.

It caused so much dislike that players unhappy with its inclusion would use scripts to automatically spit-emote on those seen riding it, resulting in Blizzard disabling the emote shortly after.

The question now is whether Blizzard will see this upheaval as an opportunity to U-turn and reapproach premium housing cosmetics, or whether it will stay the course.

#3816. Bungie’s new leadership finally understands what Destiny fans want—after we spent years shouting it at them

Is this what confidence in Bungie feels like?

Destiny 2 sure had a once-in-a-lifetime announcement this year. Three or four of them, in fact. 2026 has been a decade of a year for the game, including death, swan song, glorious rebirth, and an afterlife.

This week, Bungie detailed all it aims to bring back to the game after being cut in the past years. It’s certainly ambitious, and the studio doesn’t seem too daunted by that prospect—though having the backing of millions of players can’t hurt.

The return of the missing content by itself isn’t the key takeaway, though. For the first time in years, Bungie’s new leadership seems finally at liberty to communicate openly and sincerely with the Destiny 2 community. No half-concealed words or conveniently ignoring difficult topics, instead embracing the tough questions and finally building momentum.

Adopting this stance earlier could have meant Destiny 2 wouldn’t need awe-inspiring support from hundreds of thousands of fans to be saved. Maybe it wouldn’t need saving at all.

It’s refreshing to see the new decision-makers at Bungie being so candid, in particular about hard topics. Of course, saving the game from death through community support earns heaps of goodwill to your fans. But for the first time in a couple of years, the relationship doesn’t feel transactional, dismissive, or outright antagonistic.

Bungie’s new leadership certainly deserves credit for steering the ship during this comeback. They’re bound to run into some colossal challenges, especially once you look at the extent of everything they plan on reinstating.

But let’s face it: it wasn’t that hard to do the right thing in the first place.

I’m not saying this to hate on the new leadership (and I’m using this term broadly to define the people with decision-making power). Head of product Josh Deane, new studio head Poria Torkan, and others have absolutely been doing a great job fostering goodwill, being transparent about its big-picture plans, and sharing timelines, in no small part with the help of community manager Dylan Gafner.

Because of this new direction, I finally have faith in Bungie for the first time since The Final Shape in mid-2024. Not just because they’re doing the right things, but because, unlike the previous leaders, they’re not doing the wrong things—and for Bungie, that’s often just as important.

When you look at it, a lot of the studio’s shortcomings were self-inflicted. Siphoning resources from Destiny 2 for an uncertain bet on the nascent Marathon caused a schism that might be irreparable to the community, and the eldest of the two titles undoubtedly suffered for it. The vision for The Edge of Fate seemed borderline sadistic, cranking the power grind back to 11 and branding it as content.

Read what’s behind the latest news in gaming (with a bit of snark) by subscribing to the Destructoid Checkpoint newsletter!

Complaints about obvious pain points would go unanswered, particularly after The Edge of Fate. Players were begging for any change, but Bungie’s inaction seemed to show it was unable—or worse, unwilling—to put out fires, instead letting the house burn down. The studio appeared to either not understand or not care about the overwhelming feedback, which feels like a special skill all on its own. It’d clean house at the “worst superpower” contest, that’s for sure.

Compare it to now. One end-of-service announcement, a killer update, and millions of displays of support later, Deane told Destiny 2 fans not to buy Marathon as a donation to keep the developer afloat because “It’s our job to show up for you.” If I saw a certain CEO writing that a couple of years ago, I would’ve assumed they were either hacked, under duress, or aiming for gold at the World Series of Saying Things They Don’t Mean.

Fans sent the message loud and clear that the previous approach was unsustainable, which is why Destiny 2 is back from the dead and equipped with new people at the helm. We’ve spent years telling Bungie what not to do, and the new leadership is finally listening and taking it to heart. That’s another skill on its own, of course, especially in a community as varied as Destiny 2‘s.

Comms are cautious yet candid. The old Bungie might have blurred dates with vague “in a future update,” but the latest announcement is clear: don’t expect the unvaulting until at least early 2028. It’s imperfect and far off and difficult and not what some may have hoped to hear. But it’s real.

I’m unabashedly excited for new content for Destiny 2 again, which I haven’t been since Heresy. I don’t mind that I’ll have to wait a year and change for it. I know this time, at least it will be done right. There’s also the possible Destiny remaster and whatever’s in the future of the franchise.

It’s hard not to wonder what would have happened if maybe leadership had changed sooner, before apathy became the norm. It would have been a lot easier to wait two years if the process had started two years ago, so we’d be reaping the benefits of it now—and, as a bonus, we wouldn’t have had to watch Destiny 2 agonize.

I wish the good news hadn’t come at the cost of the game dying, but I’m glad we’re getting anything, even if it’s a bit far off. Until then, I’m confident Bungie will surprise me along the way, and I don’t even remember the last time I felt that.

Destructoid's former Destiny 2 expert (RIP), Pedro now spends way too much time concocting builds in Warframe, playing Elden Ring, or practicing guitar. He's been writing professionally since 2019 and takes psychic damage every time someone forgets an Oxford comma.

It's hard to overstate Dan's impact over the past 27 years. From shipping Project Gotham Racing on the original XBOX in 2001 to leading the creation of Forza, founding Turn 10 Studios and appearing so many times on our E3 stage, usually making a dramatic entrance with a supercar in tow—and so much more—we owe tremendous thanks and gratitude to Dan. On behalf of both teams, I would like to thank Dan for his leadership, his support, and his partnership. I wish him well for whatever comes next.

The Verge reports that Dan Greenawalt, studio head of Forza Motorsport developer Turn 10, is planning to retire after nearly 27 years, quoting an internal memo from Trevor Williams of Playground Games. "Dan Greenawalt has decided that this is the right time for him to retire from Microsoft," Williams is reported to have said, clarifying that Greenawalt will stay on temporarily as an adviser during a changeover period.

Microsoft announced in September that it plans to merge Turn 10 and Playground, the two Forza studios, into one entity as part of the same restructure that will merge Obsidian into Bethesda and hand Halo over to Activision. Oh, and that restructure will also see another 268 employees being laid off.

Turn 10 had already been turned into a support studio for Playground's Forza Horizon following the 2023 reboot of Forza Motorsport, with former developer Fred Russell saying last year that the Motorsport series died in a prior round of cuts at Microsoft.

Considering the year Zendaya is having, it feels inevitable that her roles in various projects on the 2026 movie schedule will inspire Halloween costumes. However, when it comes to her own costume, she’s dressing up as another iconic actress: Halle Berry. In fact, she channeled her so well that I actually thought she was Halle Berry for a second.

Seeing as Zendaya has been rocking a pixie cut these days, she was already giving Halle Berry in the early 2000s vibes. So, for Halloween, she capitalized on that. In a post from her stylist, Law Roach, they showed how they recreated Berry’s look from the 2000 New York premiere of X-Men; take a look:

As you can see, the Spider-Man: Brand New Day star is rocking a matching yellow, silver, and white Lanvin set from 2000 that is made up of a triangle bikini top and low-rise bootcut pants. She’s also rocking a cute pair of sunglasses that scream early-2000s.

Seriously, she looks stunning, and honestly, exactly like Halle Berry! In fact, she looks so much like the X-Men actress that I thought it was her for a second. However, after a double take, I realized it was, in fact, Zendaya, and she just has a remarkable resemblance to the woman known for playing Storm, especially now that she has super short hair.

Berry was seriously impressed by this fit too, as she commented on Roach’s post:

Now, while this look and Zendaya’s resemblance to Berry in these photos came as a shock at first, upon some reflection, it’s really not surprising that she did this at all. The actresses are good friends, Berry has sung Zendaya’s praises on many occasions, and this is not the first time the Dune actress has created a major celebrity fashion moment inspired by the Monster’s Ball star.

In fact, she paid homage to Berry a month ago at the Emmys, as Law Roach told Refinery 29. In that instance, the 2026 Emmy nominee was rocking a beautiful custom dress by Prada that was covered in diamonds. It resembled the sparkling silver dress the Oscar winner wore to the premiere of Die Another Day in 2002, per People.

Well, now that Zendaya has shown she can perfectly channel Halle Berry on more than one occasion, I’d love to see the Crime 101 star recreate one of The Drama actress's iconic fashion moments. This year alone, The Odyssey star has shown off that she’s the master of method dressing on countless occasions as she’s promoted three movies. However, for now, I’ll be admiring how Zendaya recreated a Halle Berry look so well that I actually thought she was Halle Berry for a second.

#3812. "A cold dead place that's slowly decaying" - EA employees reveal a culture of secrecy and terrible morale following layoffs

Last week, EA announced it's laying off 400 workers across multiple studios, cancelling projects and refocusing on its biggest money-makers. As part of that, EA closed down the iconic BioWare studio, letting go of most of its remaining staff of around 50 people.

The mood inside EA is, unsurprisingly, low. Speaking to Vertical Slice, a number of current and former staff revealed a culture of secrecy surrounding layoffs, and a lack of clarity on who, exactly, is affected and how their teams are meant to move forward without them.

"My suspicion is that it is done to isolate the people laid off," one source said. "Depending on how large a layoff it is, it can take us a week or two or more to get our bearings back under us and figure out what we're doing."

This also affects the work itself, since in-progress projects become the responsibility of the fewer remaining members of the team. But a source revealed that it can take weeks for EA to communicate those specifics to staff and to chart a path forward.

EA's approach to telling affected employees they're being let go is one that should sound familiar to anyone who knows the modern corporate world. According to multiple sources, staff are invited to a Zoom call with chat disabled and the other participants hidden. They're then told they're being laid off, without being given the chance to ask any questions or say goodbye to their colleagues.

"You're getting laid off because you're just numbers on a list," one source said. " There's never an understanding of the actual project [you're working on]."

Sources also said EA is prioritising profits over the wellbeing of its people, now more than ever. As a result of EA's $55bn acquisition by a consortium of investors - chiefly Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund - EA is saddled with $20bn of debt it has to find ways to recoup.

"Morale has been terrible," another source said. "The line we kept hearing is 'do less, better' but it just felt like we were doing the same amount with less people. Upper management was very excited about Claude and the possibilities of [generative] AI, much to the chagrin of my team."

For the largest game publisher in the western world, all of this is unfortunate to see. But for many within EA, the decline has been seeping in for a while.

"That the recent email about the organisation changes [sounded like] it was written by a robot best sums up EA," one source said. "A cold dead place that's slowly decaying as leadership pilfers every last cent, leaving the rest of us to worry about how we feed our families."

Meanwhile, elsewhere in the games industry, the Xbox division is suffering through multiple waves of lay-offs, all with the cumulative aim of removing 3,200 people from their roles. Raj Patel, who's been tracking games industry layoffs, recently revealed on Bluesky that 2026 is on track to be the worst year on record in terms of the number of people laid off.

SPOILERS lie ahead for Scrubs latest episode “My Halloween,” now streaming with a Hulu subscription.

I’ve really been enjoying the Scrubs revival ever since it premiered early this year, but man, this refreshing second season is really entertaining. Every episode has felt like another highlight on the jam-packed 2026 TV schedule, but this week reminded me how good the medical comedy is at tackling more serious topics, while also keeping me laughing. With that, I have to talk about being caught off guard by one sobering moment.

Late in Season 1, viewers learned that Dr. Cox was suffering from an incurable autoimmune disease. And then, at the beginning of Season 2, it's revealed that his insurance is not being completely covered for the treatments he needs. While I was happy to see Dr. Cox back for the first time since the Season 2 premiere, I was dismayed that it was for a troubling reason.

As the episode unfolds, it's established that Dr. Cox has taken up a role as a concierge doctor, where he has to deal with a lot of buffoonery due to an entitled CEO. When J.D. asks Dr. Cox what’s going on, he explains it as follows:

J.D., I didn’t come back here because I was bored. I came back here, because even with insurance I am drowning in medical bills. The fact of the matter is, I came back here because I need this job… I had so many plans for my golden years, but all those plans are gone, and I did everything that I was supposed to do, and then I got sick. And, here I am.

Dr. Cox has had an entire career as a physician of internal medicine, who J.D. has known as the Chief of Medicine at Sacred Heart Hospital. Since he’s in his sixties, Cox deserves a restful retirement where he doesn’t have to worry about money and working anymore. However, I’m impressed that Scrubs takes an opportunity to bring up this common problem for retirees. Many of them are forced to go back into the workforce in order to survive, and Dr. Cox is no exception.

I think the show does an excellent job of showing Dr. Cox’s disappointment in the healthcare system, whilst also making the show as entertaining as ever. Yeah, this kind of tricky, thematic balance is why I love Scrubs.

The more dramatic turn for Dr. Cox is definitely a highlight, but there's another jump scare of a topic in “My Halloween” as well. Dr. Elliot Reid is trying to make a difference as a doctor and sets up her own women’s clinic, but no one seems to care. She tries to recruit some other doctors, and thinks since the new hospital administrator, Cassie, is a woman, she might care enough to put her plan through. However, she simply shuts her down because she doesn’t believe investing in women’s healthcare is going to make the hospital money. Oof!

I won’t go on a heated rant about how women’s healthcare is treated, but just like the Dr. Cox arc, I’m so amazed Scrubs was able to make a solid point about the healthcare system all while being filled with a bunch of funny moments, too. Given those serious developments as well as the fallout of Elliot’s recent romance gone wrong and the debut of Elliot and J.D.’s kid, I'm hooked for the rest of the season.

Check out Scrubs when it airs on Wednesdays at 8 p.m. ET on ABC as part of the 2026 TV schedule.

#3809. Complete Probably Stolen walkthrough: Week one

Probably Stolen is much more than running your cyberpunk-themed store, since you’ll come across unique NPCs. Not only will they make personal requests, but some of them will also hand you crucial clues along the way.

In this guide, I will discuss all the events that will take place across two in-game weeks.

The first week is where you begin your trade and set up your shop. First, pick a Specialization from the complete list of options available. Easiest one is Apprentice if you want things to begin smoothly.

Next, pick the starting Perks you want to shape your save. Similarly, you can pick from three different difficulty modifier options. The game will give you a quick tutorial of the overlay, and you’re all set then for your first piece of business.

There will be five customers to attend, and you can call them using the green button near the recorder. At first, you’ll find your mentor who guides you about the basics. The customers who appear will be randomized, so the ones I encountered will be different from the ones you do.

Ideally, I looked to buy all types of food items since they can be sold for a profit. You’ll also be provided with a list of criminals; if one of them appears, make sure to inform the authorities. This specific encounter is fixed for all players.

The same pattern follows, and you will have four customers to attend to. Once again, I looked to purchase any food item they had, or discounted stuff they looked to sell for cheap. Do note that not every discounted item will be profitable, but you ultimately go green eventually.

After the second day, you’ll be able to visit the Dumping Ground. Once you exhaust all attempts, pick the most valuable item and return.

On the third day, you’ll have six customers to attend. However, one of them will be your mentor, and you’ll learn about how to check discrepancies. You can use your magnifying glass to inspect closely whether the product you’re about to buy has any defects or not.

On the fourth day, you’ll come across the labeler. The labeler allows you to fix counterfeit items that raise their values. I also came across one of the six criminals notified on that day and decided to call the authorities.

On the fifth day, you’ll get to establish your display case. You can keep an assorted list of items in it. Do note that the types of items you keep will attract different kind of customers to your shop. On my run, a second bounty target appeared, and I once again decided to call the authorities on them.

The sixth day didn’t have anything worthwhile happening during my run. By now, you should find some really valuable items to purchase from a few customers. If you have the credits, don’t hesitate to buy them.

The final day of the first week has the highest number of clients to meet. Moreover, you’ll get to encounter someone named Wild, and you’ll learn about upgrades. Known as Wild’s Favours, you can pick from a wide variety of improvements.

Your picks will largely depend on how your run is proceeding and what kind of items you need.

Stay tuned for the walkthrough for the second week and all its days.

I've played about 50+ hours of the World of Warcraft: Forever beta, and wouldn't you know it, I'm going to be playing a lot more when it comes out November 4.

Earlier this week, Kris Zierhut, principal game designer on World of Warcraft: Forever, said that the game would have a release schedule that's a "little more laid back". Rather than the blisteringly fast eight to 10 week schedule of Season of Discovery, Forever'll aim to release major updates once every four months or so.

This is honestly music to my ears—I've been impressed by retail WoW's blistering pace and its seasonal structure, even if there have been some rocky, bug-filled patches in the past; and it's certainly something I've praised before, especially in contrast to other certain MMOs that have been coming to a standstill.

But I've been playing WoW… well, for a long time, but I've had a consistent sub since Dragonflight, and I've been able to see the arc of Blizzard whipping up its schedule into a proper roadmap. Which did pull the game back from the brink, true, but three expansions in and I'm just sort of exhausted.

There's always some new bar to fill, some new doohickey to collect, some new reputation track to chew on, and it all moves so fast that if I, say, have an off-week to go play another game, I feel pretty lost. While Midnight does major patches at roughly the same release tempo (12.0.0 came out in January, 12.1.0 came out in August) it also has a ton of interim stuff to flood out your schedule every three months, rather than four.

Launch was already crammed with stuff—a raid tier, delves, the new prey system, housing, and so on. Just under three months passed since launch, and wham, suddenly we've got Void Assaults! Ritual Sites! The Omnium Folio! Whatever Abyss Anglers is, I never checked, which is kinda the problem! Just over a month later, and there's a new raid and a new system plugged into Void Assaults (which I'm literally just now finding out about, I completely missed it). Two months later, and it's 12.1.0, which I hadn't even sat down to properly play before Labyrinths became a thing.

The idea of smaller, chiller patches in an overall slower-paced game (here's fellow PCG writer Lincoln Carpenter's treatise on the virtues of hitting a scorpion with a club for 38 seconds) sounds like a nice, soothing bath after an overstimulating day at the circus.

I do feel that prickling sense of overstimulation fear return when Zierhut talks about the interim stuff, however:

Keep up to date with the most important stories and the best deals, as picked by the PC Gamer team.

"And then one nuance on that is: We do plan on making content that unlocks in between … you want to stagger out some content across those four months. It's not just patch day comes [around], here's a content fire hose, and now we're silent for four months. A lot of that is, hey, there's a time event calendar that gradually unlocks things and opens them up over those four months to give things a little bit more life instead of that all at once effect."

Still, given Forever's meant to be a horizontally-progressing game that doesn't have expansions (we'll need to see how that pans out), I might find these little tasks a lot more soothing than the looming feeling I have with WoW, where at any point it might suddenly become too late to get stuck into a season.

Ideally, these mid-patch trickles will be optional tasks I can get around to basically whenever, rather than something I feel pressured to get done just so I can stay up-to-date for whatever flashy system's trundling down the pipeline next. Hit me with that lo-fi update cadence, I'm ready for it.

HBO’s Harry Potter show has sparked more than a few thoughts amongst Wizarding World fans, with much of that discussion centered around the new cast. One of the biggest ongoing discussions has to do with the casting of Professor Severus Snape, who’s being played by Paapa Essiedu. Unfortunately, the seasoned British actor has received significant backlash and even death threats for taking on the role. Essiedu has taken the negative commentary in stride, however, and he recently shared a refreshing take on it as well.

Much of the criticism surrounding Essiedu’s Snape casting has to do with the fact that he’s of African descent. In J.K. Rowling’s books, Snape is described as being Caucasian and is also depicted as such in the original films, where he’s played by the late Alan Rickman. Essiedu, for his part, is fully aware of the chatter surrounding him and, based on his recent chat with Variety at the Time100 Next Gala, he seemingly knew such blowback would occur. Nevertheless, the star isn’t focusing on the vitriol but something else instead:

The whole team has been so supportive of me. Obviously, my priority is the work. I wouldn’t take this job on [otherwise], but I walk into it with open eyes. I understand the broad spectrum of what the reaction to what we’re doing means, and I take that mantle on with an open and full heart. I’ve also been blown away by a lot of the support and well-wishes and excitement.

Now, that’s what I call exuding grace under fire. What the Gangs of London alum seems to have struck is a firm balance when it comes to acknowledging the backlash. He certainly remains cognizant of it and isn’t remaining ignorant to what people are saying. Nevertheless, he wisely seems to be choosing not to remain fixated on it. I also love that he’s also choosing to zero in on the more positive aspects of the situation, as there are indeed those who are supportive and are open to him taking on Snape.

Even though Paapa Essiedu seems to have a level-headed take on some of the more brutal responses to his hiring, it’s still unfortunate that he’s had to contend with such remarks at all. What’s been encouraging to see, though, is that the producers behind Harry Potter are taking those death threats very seriously by providing the necessary training and security. Additionally, Essiedu has been receiving support from fellow HP alums, with one being Jason Isaacs. The Lucius Malfoy icon spoke in defense of Essiedu amid the backlash.

Essiedu was tapped for the role of Snape around early 2025, and there remained considerable curiosity as to how he would look in character. The first images hinted at what appeared to be a somewhat smoother-looking Snape complete with dreads. At this point, Essiedu isn’t exactly keen on calling his character a style icon, but he’s not made at the praise for the costuming:

I think the aesthetic is important. I don’t know if style is necessarily at the forefront of my mind when generating the character, but I think the way he looks tells so much about who he is — and who he wants people to think he is. It’s all incredibly well thought through and collaborated with the incredible costume department.

At this point, I’m more than ready to see how Paapa Essiedu brings his own flair to the role of Snape. We’ll see that when Harry Potter premieres on HBO (and debuts for HBO Max subscription holders as well) on Christmas Day amid the 2026 TV schedule. In the meantime, hopefully, Essiedu will continue to be able to maintain his personal peace amid the sea of unpleasant comments.

"We apologize to players who have been kindly awaiting the release of this title"

FromSoftware's The Duskbloods - a game that is best described as Bloodborne meets Sekiro meets Dark Souls, with jetpacks and dinos thrown in - has been delayed from its 2026 launch window into an unspecified time in 2027.

"While development of The Duskbloods is at the final adjustment stage, we have made the decision to move the launch window to 2027," says a tweet from the game's official Twitter account. "We apologise to players who have been kindly awaiting the release of this title and thank you for your patience and support."

A follow-up message continued: "During the network test, we saw active interest in the core concepts of the game, including combat, strategic depth, and player expression. To further enhance these aspects, we have decided to move the launch, allowing time for final adjustments to game rules and balancing."

There was a suggestion previously that the title may have launched in September, but the prospective date for the unannounced release came and went without ceremony. Many consumers were uncertain whether the game would ever make its vague '2026' release window, given we've heard nothing from either publisher Nintendo or developer FromSoft since August's playtests.

Appetite for the game is ravenous, it seems: in the aforementioned closed network test, more people applied to try the game out than Elden Ring Nightreign - and that's an impressive stat, considering The Duskbloods is only launching on Switch 2.

But maybe a bit more time in the oven is a good thing for this peculiar, experimental title: the network test hasn't been without problems, as the first session ended abruptly following major connectivity issues. Though these were ironed out by the later sessions, here's hoping a full launch will be a little more stable than that.

#3804. How to access the Pirate Shop and get Tokens in Fortnite

One of the biggest features of the Treasure Hunters season in Fortnite is now live, and we can finally access the Pirate Shop. While it might look like the standard store, there’s a key difference: everything you find inside is available for free.

That’s right, you can pick anything you want from the shelves without any additional resources. But first, you need to get access to the shop.

You can gain access to the Pirate Shop between Nov. 1 and Dec. 5, throughout the course of the Treasure Hunters season. You can obtain any item inside the store priced in V-Bucks for free. To gain access, you need to find Pirate Shop Tokens.

These special tokens come in two types. One of them allows you to activate it any time until Dec. 15, 2026. You can activate the other at any point between Jan. 1 and Dec. 15, 2027.

Once you activate a token, you have 14 days to claim everything you can find in the Item Shop. Bundles and items that cost real-life money are an exception to this rule, but it’s still a wonderful opportunity.

To find these valuable tokens, you’ll need to watch out for special chests. These chests don’t have fixed locations, and their odds appear to be quite low. Once you find one, open them. If you’re lucky, you’ll receive access to the Pirate Shop as a reward.

If you’re playing as a squad, you just need to find one treasure chest. All teammates will receive access to the Pirate Shop as long as one of them has obtained the tokens. This also incentivizes you to play the season in squads, since you’ll (theoretically) have higher chances to hit gold.

"The number of downloads and purchases has *not* doubled."

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

It seems it isn't just Steam that's being flooded with AI slop. Indie games storefront itch.io has reported that the number of new game pages being created per day on the site has doubled in the past two months, and just like Valve's much bigger distribution service, the finger is being pointed at AI.

Over on Bluesky, itch.io shared an image of a bar chart labelled "game events". The chart shows that, between August 3 and October 30, the number of new game pages being created per day has risen from around 3,000 to regularly surpassing 6,000. It's a ratio that more or less matches the increase in Steam demos showcased at the most recent Next Fest, which rose from around 4,000 to over 8,000.

While Itch doesn't explicitly point the finger at AI as the cause, it heavily infers it. When Bluesky user Tommy's Homemade Games asked "Do you know why?" Itch responded "take a guess" followed by emojis of a crying face and a robot. Another Bluesky account, BardZaku, asked "is it AI dreck?" to which the account replied with an emoji of a face with bags under its eyes.

The rapid uptick in Itch pages also coincides with the launch of Claude Opus 5, which arrived on July 24. The latest iteration of Anthropic's LLM—which is now at version 5.5—has proved particularly adept at reverse engineering code. This has had a bunch of knock-on effects in various areas of game development, ranging from much faster decompilations of old games, to Steam being flooded with AI slop, and developers cancelling public demos out of concerns their games will be cloned.

Anthropic has since updated Claude to reign in its ability to directly copy games, but it's currently hard to tell whether it has stemmed the broader flow of AI generated games. Indeed, it's worth pointing out that AI Generated games now comprise a good portion of the pages listed on Itch. Out of 1,769,316 listed on Itch at the time of writing, 131,929 are tagged as AI Generated, approximately 7.5% of the total. That's a lot, considering how long AI coding tools have been around.

But to play devil's advocate, Itch is a storefront that allows AI games, and if people are downloading and enjoying these games, then adding them to the store is fair enough, right? Well, Itch also points out that, although the number of games appearing on Itch per day has doubled, "the number of downloads and purchases has *not* doubled". This suggests these AI games are clogging up the site for nobody's benefit, not even the people 'making' them.

The question, then, is what's to be done about all this? The replies to Itch's initial post are filled with calls to ban AI generated games from the store. But as pointed out by AI researcher Mike Cook, simply banning these games is unlikely to solve the problem.

From the creators of Edge: A free weekly videogame industry newsletter, featuring in-depth news, expert analysis and exclusive interviews

"I think that would be a good move. But it won't change this graph, unfortunately," Cook wrote on Bluesky. "You need a team of people to enforce it, or a very dicey public reporting system. Even then, it's a lot harder to detect than people think." Valve has also cast doubt on the efficacy of a ban on AI coding tools for games released on Steam, though its opinion is heavily influenced by the company's laissez-faire approach to operating its storefront.

Another possibility is to simply let this trend play out. There is a viral element to the ongoing surge in AI generated games, as people post their vibe-coded works online for attention and social media clout. But Itch's statement suggests that people aren't properly engaging with most of the games being uploaded.

Hence, it's possible that the people behind these games may eventually lose interest, moving on to whatever attention-grabbing scheme big tech facilitates next. The risk, of course, is that the audience also loses interest in what these storefronts offer before that happens. After all, nobody wants to wade through a tsunami of slop to get to the games they want to play.

Everybody’s been sad, but not everybody has dealt with depression. I have, when I lost my mother, and I was in a really dark place.

Gradually, I’ve come to heal, and I now smile more than I tear up when I think about her. That said, do you know what helped get me through my dark period? Watching movies about depression. In a sense, it helped me to feel my way through my own grief.

Well, one series that snuck up on me is the anime, This Monster Wants to Eat Me. It’s currently available with a Crunchyroll subscription, and it’s definitely one of the most unique representations of depression I’ve ever seen. Here’s why.

One thing I love about anime is that it can often tackle heavy subject matter in the form of the supernatural. My favorite anime, Attack on Titan, tackled fascism, racism, and discrimination, and had them all on display while people zipped around on wires and cut giants on their napes. Sure, American cartoons have delved into adult territories, too (Avatar: The Last Airbender tackled genocide. The new show, Avatar: Seven Havens addresses P.T.S.D.) But, I think there’s something to anime specifically as a lot of it is not meant for children.

This Monster Wants to Eat Me is no exception. The main character, Hinako, lost her entire family in a car crash, and she’s the sole survivor. Oftentimes, it’s a struggle for her to even get out of bed, and her sole ambition is to see her family again. In other words, she contemplates joining them. However, a yokai, which is a Japanese spirit, in the form of a mermaid, wants to eat Hinako, because her blood is apparently delicious.

And this, of course, can be interpreted as a metaphor for depression itself being an all-consuming monster. Hinako eventually befriends the Yokai because it promises to eventually eat her one day. Make of that what you will.

I’ve been thinking a lot about RJ Miite ever since he died by suicide. Like many fans of his work, it hit me hard. But, what hit me even harder was when I heard stories about his former coworkers hanging out with him just days before he died. Some of them could tell that something was wrong, but they never imagined that he would take his own life. It was a shock to many.

This Monster Wants to Eat Me reveals what a support system looks like for somebody with suicidal thoughts, but that as much as they try, the grief, i.e., the monster, might be too much to contend with. Hinako’s best friend is a spunky redhead named Miko. Now, Miko can be a bit much when it comes to her exuberance, but we later learn that it’s all an act. Being there for her friend takes a lot out of her.

Miko just wants Hinako to be happy, though, and she goes through any length to protect her…even if she’s not exactly what she seems. I’ll just leave it at that. Aside from being a great show about depression, it has lots of twists and turns.

I love this anime’s story, but what I love the most is that it truly captures the FEELING of depression.

There is a lot of cheeriness and fake smiles going on here, but underneath it all are the quiet moments. Most of the characters are both literally and figuratively hiding their true selves, and that’s very much what depression feels like. The world keeps moving, even if you don’t want to keep moving with it.

I highly recommend that you watch This Monster Wants to Eat Me, but only if you’re in an emotionally safe place currently. It goes to some pretty dark places.

Rich is a Jersey boy, through and through. He graduated from Rutgers University (Go, R.U.!), and thinks the Garden State is the best state in the country. That said, he’ll take Chicago Deep Dish pizza over a New York slice any day of the week. Don’t hate. When he’s not watching his two kids, he’s usually working on a novel, watching vintage movies, or reading some obscure book.

#3800. EA's sale to Saudi-led consortium was "final nail in the coffin" for BioWare, says studio co-founder

"I'm not saying it doesn't hurt and doesn't suck."

One of BioWare's famous doctor-founders, Greg Zeschuk, has finally spoken about the studio's closure last week, saying it's "kind of sad" and that EA's leveraged buyout by a Saudi-involved consortium "was the final nail in the coffin".

Speaking to 80 Level, Zeschuk - who founded BioWare in 1995 with fellow medical students Ray Muzyka and Augustine Yip - said he was fishing when news of the studio's closure broke. "I got like 10 texts," Zeschuk said. "I came off the river and got to my little room and opened my phone, and it's like, 'I'm so sorry to hear about BioWare.' And I'm like, 'Oh shit.'"

By the time he flew home later, he'd already apparently digested the news and missed most of the discourse around it. "I wasn't there to share in the moment," he said, "which in some ways was nice because I was able to kind of just take my time with it.

"I'm not saying it doesn't hurt and doesn't suck," he added. "And I think it's kind of sad. It's actually, in some ways, saddest for the city of Edmonton, where we're from, because we were kind of this beacon of hope and excitement and possibility. We showed you could do something really special in a place that was not known for doing things like that."

Zeschuk and Muzyka retired from BioWare in 2012, the year Mass Effect 3 was released, so they've been away from the business for a considerable amount of time. They've moved on. "I've kind of gone through all the emotions long, long ago," Zeschuk explained.

BioWare did change thereafter, he seemed to accept, but as a result of a gradual change propelled naturally by people leaving and other people coming in. "I'm not going to have so much hubris to say Ray and I were the lynchpin in the chain, our departure ruined everything," he said. "It wasn't that at all. It's a slow and insidious kind of thing and again, it's the people. The people are the key."

When he heard the private acquisition of EA had gone through, that's when he feared things might be headed to a bad place. "I think it was the final nail in the coffin," he said. "I think that was the crux of it in a sense. BioWare makes these kinds of unusual games that take a long time and they're complicated and so it's easier just to pump out sports games every year, and that's a better business model in some ways."

Elsewhere in the interview, Zeschuk talked a little about the origins of BioWare selling to EA in 2008 - "We had options actually" - and about personally sliding away from story-driven games towards more action-centred games like the Nioh series and Elden Ring.

Since 2017, Zeschuk has been building a beer-brewing company called Blind Enthusiasm, which apparently now employs a dozen people and ships tens of thousands of bottles of beer a year. This interview is the only one Zeschuk has given. Muzyka has so far declined to be interviewed. The third BioWare co-founder, Augustine Yip, left the company long ago, back in 1998.

#3799. Oh No, Who Turned Out The Lights In Anor Londo?!

I’ve been playing Dark Souls recently, getting much farther than I ever have before and enjoying myself greatly. Two days ago, after several attempts and a run back to the sewers to farm some rats for Humanity, I finally defeated the infamous Ornstein and Smough (as well as the jackasses that guard the room they hang out in) and was able to proceed into what I’m told is the second half of the game.

But first, the finale of the first act: upstairs from Ornstein and Smough is a chamber, golden light overflowing into the hallway outside. On the approach, numerous player-provided warnings of “Chest ahead” were scrawled across every free inch of the floor. Inside, an enormous woman with an enormous bosom reclining on a platform was gazing benevolently at me. Once I drew close, an action appeared: Kneel.

This is Gwynevere, the Princess of Sunlight. She’s here to reward me for all my hard work! You see, I’m the Chosen Undead, and I’m here to collect the Lordvessel so I can usher in a new Age of Fire, or something like that. That’s what everyone keeps telling me, anyway. Gwynevere gives me the vessel and sends me off on my way with gushing praise for my work so far, sweet prayers for my future success, and a soaring triumphant soundtrack to make sure I know I’m a good little Undead doing good work out there in service of the Flame or Sun or whatever.

That’s nice, Gwynevere. That’s real nice. So why does this whole roomÂ stink to high heaven?!

As alluded to above, I have never finished Dark Souls. I’ve absorbed bits of it by cultural osmosis: I know there’s a choice of some sort at the end, I’ve seen clips of some boss fights like Four Kings and Seath the Scaleless. I know that my buddy Solaire is probably going to die and that I can save him, but I’m not 100-percent sure how. But I don’t really know what any of this Sun Princess stuff is about. What I do know is what I’ve learned from playing hours of Elden Ring and Elden Ring: Nightreign, and dabbling in King’s Field 4 and now this game:Â nothing should be this cheery. There is absolutely no sincere reason in a game like this that a shining woman with ample bosom should be waiting in a room like this to reward me like this is some sort of cartoon Camelot. And what’s with the music, man?! This game isÂ silent except for the overtuned sound effects, Firelink Shrine, and the screaming choruses of boss battles. This entire businessÂ reeks, but I don’t know why, nor what to do about it.

Which is why I have to thank whichever benevolent adventurer scrawled, amidst all the jokes about boobs on the floor of Gwynevere’s room, “Try attacking.”

This single message has demolished me internally for two whole days. I have never once, unprovoked, with murderous intent in my heart, killed an NPC in a FromSoftware game. In fact, I can count on one hand the number of innocent NPCs I’ve killed in games ever (unless you include Everhood, whoops). I tried to start a genocide run in Undertale once and gave up after three battles. I once accidentally whapped the Turtle Pope in Elden Ring on the head and instantly shut off my system and reloaded. I’ll make a morally grey choice once in a while in games, sure, but murder? Out of the question!

Which is why it has floored me how much brain space the prospect of murdering this sun goddess lady has taken up lately! Dark Souls is notorious for telling you very, very little about what’s really going on. You’ve got to piece together the lore from context clues, scant dialogue, and item descriptions if you want to understand why people are behaving the way they are behaving, or why you’re in the mess you’re in. I’m not a lore fiend, so while I try to pay attention, I have not dedicated myself in any capacity to understanding what the hell Anor Londo’s whole deal is. I don’t really have good reason, at this stage, to mistrust any of the things anyone’s telling me. I was told to ring some bells to open a path, and that happened when I did. I was told to go collect the Lordvessel, and I did that too. All the people I’ve been instructed to kill so far have, by and large, seemed like pretty effed-up dudes. And everyone who is giving me instructions has been very nice! Benevolent, even, in a world where everything seemed deeply messed up and kindness is in short supply. Heck, Solaire worships the sun, right? Surely the sun princess is fine, then?

Agh. I couldn’t get the idea out of my head. I stalled. I went back to Undead Asylum and fell through the floor. I got sucked into a painting for a bit, and offered mercy to a lady dressed in white who insisted the inhabitants of her world (who were outside crucifying one another seemingly) were kind and good. But I feel instinctively like some mysterious clock is ticking. I really want to decide whether or not I’m going to do what these guys keep telling me to doÂ before I mosey on out there and start collecting great souls or whatever to feed this Lordvessel thing.

I love, love, love when games get into my head like this. I love the uncertainty, the pressure to make a meaningful decision. It helps that I know, from playing Elden Ring, that FromSoftware loves to put players in these sorts of challenging positions, where there is no easy nor obvious “right” thing to do, but where we must live with whatever decision we make anyway. It’s why I’ve elected to learn very little about the rest of the story before I move on. I want to save Solaire, but I don’t want someone else to tell me how. I want to see what Siegmeyer’s up to, but if I can’t manage to find him, that’s my own fault. The game goes on. Perfection is unobtainable. Just like in life.

So while I don’t want to “ruin” my game by doing something evil, if I don’t shoot this buxom golden temptress, I won’t get to personally experience whatever twisted consequence Dark Souls has for that choice. Then again, maybe it’s nothing. Maybe I’ll shoot her and literally nothing will happen. She’s a god or something, right? Probably immortal? It’s probably fine?

Chronicles: Medieval is an impressive looking open-world sandbox where players explore a dynamic Medieval world and fight in massive, authentic battles. It's been in development for more than four years and is due to launch into Steam early access early in 2027.

However, there is a very real chance this will no longer happen, as developer Raw Power Games suddenly faces closure after funding for its game was pulled.

On Friday, Raw Power Games posted a statement to Steam and on social media channels (via IGN), explaining how the studio has suddenly found itself in dire straits. "Due to circumstances outside our control, the necessary funding for Raw Power Games is no longer in place," the studio wrote. "Without it, we can't keep building Chronicles: Medieval, and right now the studio is at real risk of closing."

This appears to be a sudden development. Through October, the studio had been posting regular development updates, including an incredibly detailed deep dive on Medieval coats of arms and how they would appear in the game. None of it suggested a studio that's in trouble, so it seems this has caught Raw Power off guard.

By the sounds of it, Chronicles: Medieval isn't all that far away from being done, either. Or at least ready for its planned alpha launch: "What makes it hurt is how close we are. Early access is within reach," Raw Power Games writes in its statement. "The world we've been building for years is finally starting to feel alive, and we have so much we've been thrilled to show you."

Chronicles: Medieval first appeared on our radar last year, not without some controversy. At the time, Raw Power Games was super excited about using generative AI for its games. Not only was the studio using Midjourney to generate (terrible) concept art, but company COO Jakob Rasmussen told Danish newspaper Ingeniøren that genAI was "at the core of our vision", adding that "When the technology is ready—and perhaps a little sooner—we'll be willing to stick our necks out and put it into the game."

Yet the company quickly changed its tune on this point, with CTO Caspar Strandbygaard telling PC Gamer that Chronicles: Medieval was "100% handcrafted with no use of generative AI." Strandbygaard admitted that Raw Power was still "curious" about the technology, but regarding Chronicles specifically, he stressed that "every asset in the game is built by our extremely talented team of passionate developers. It is not generated by AI."

Keep up to date with the most important stories and the best deals, as picked by the PC Gamer team.

While the situation seems grim for Raw Power, the studio says that it is "not going down without a fight" and has urged fans of the game to "keep Chronicles: Medieval on your wishlist and keep talking about it." How much road Raw Power has remaining before it's forced to close isn't clear. But since the game is allegedly close to being in a releasable state, it may be able to secure new funding relatively soon.

#3797. How to solve the Frog Statue Puzzle in Fortnite

The Treasure Hunters season is live in Fortnite, with some cool Easter eggs to solve. This includes frog statues that are positioned centrally on the new map. Once you find them, you can solve an interesting puzzle to get rare loot. I’ll explain how the process works in this guide.

The frog statue puzzles are actually pretty easy to locate. There are three statues you have to interact with, and they are all scattered around the center island. The location is just south of Lantern Landing, and you cannot miss it if you’re heading to the middle of the map. I have also marked the spot to make it easy for you to find.

When you enter the area, you will find three statues, all turned away from the center island. To solve the puzzle, you have to interact with all of them and make them face the middle.

The key is to turn all three statues towards the center island. To do so, interact with each of the statues four times. When you do so, the statues will turn towards the center. All three statues are located at the same location, and you can find them around the center island.

Once you solve the puzzle, the Rare Chests will spawn around the well in the middle. What you find will depend on your luck, but you might get the valuable Pirate Shop access tokens.

The next live-action remake among Disney's upcoming movies is Tangled, and we just got an exciting update about where the production is at: shooting has officially wrapped! While the movie still has a long way to go before it hits theaters, the milestone is absolutely worth celebrating. Anyone up for kicking it at The Snuggly Duckling later?

The news was revealed by the movie’s co-writer Michael Montemayor. Check out his celebratory post:

A post shared by Mikey Montemayor (@mikeymontemayor)

I’m sure the whole cast and crew felt just like Rapunzel on the day she stepped out of her tower after the massive accomplishment. It’s wild that we started this year learning that Milo Manheim and Teagan Croft were cast as Flynn and Rapunzel, and now they’ve completed their journey bringing these beloved characters to life.

CinemaBlend had a chance to talk to Manheim prior to filming, and he told us he was most excited for the “I Have A Dream” sequence. Now, we’re curious what scene ended up being a highlight for everyone.

Another very exciting actor in the cast is Kathryn Hahn, and she'll be playing Mother Gothel, which fans “manifested” for her before it became a reality. Rogue One’s Diego Luna is also in the cast as a new character, and Outlander’s Caitríona Balfe is set to play Rapunzel’s mom alongside Elliot Cowan, who’s playing Corona’s king. It is being directed by Michael Gracey, who famously helmed The Greatest Showman.

During D23's Entertainment Showcase, a first look was shown. Check it out below:

We also know that both animal sidekicks will be adapted for the live-action movie. The last slide of Montemayor's post shows a funny little green stand-in for the chameleon they must have used on set before the VFX team adds Pascal in. We’ve also seen glimpses of Maximus on the set, too.

The live-action Tangled has been filming primarily in multiple locations around Spain for the past five months. The production also reportedly went to Gironde, France – where it is rumored that they filmed the “I See The Light” sequence at the Château de la Brede castle, per a post on X.

Since they’ve been filming a lot on practical sets, there have been some leaks about how the production is looking that show that the live-action adaptation is really aiming to make us feel like we’re watching the animated movie.

The new Tangled cast has also been given a lot of support by some of the original cast members from the animated movie. #3793. Sam Altman Thinks It’s Good If You Can’t Afford RAM For Your PC

If you’ve tried to buy new electronics recently, from gaming consoles to iPhones, you’ll have dealt with prices that are hundreds higher than they were even a year ago. That’s because the price of RAM keeps going up as AI companies race to build out datacenters to feed the insatiable compute demands of frontier LLM models. Lots of people think being unable to buy RAM for consumer products at a reasonable price is a bad thing. OpenAI’s Sam Altman disagrees.

âA lot of people want local inference,” the executive whose company is expected to go public sometime next year recently told the Cheeky Pint podcast. “And somehow, they assume that the problem is solved now because we are going to have open-source models, weâre going to be able to run them on our computers, and so weâre not going to need all the stuff in the data center.”

There’s a debate in the AI world right now about whether the future will be people running “light weight” open-source models on local devices, like phones and laptops, or whether all meaningful AI models will be run out of the cloud, i.e. massive data centers controlled exclusively by tech giants. Altman is coming down firmly on the side of the datacenters, and thus the companies currently buying up all available memory and sending prices skyrocketing for years to come in the process.

“But from a global allocation perspective, actually, itâs quite terrible to have everybody have a bunch of the worldâs limited supply of DRAM sitting in their own computer and being used five percent of the time,” Altman continued. “You want maximum utilization in the cloud if youâre trying to deal with this very supply constrained environment. And somehow everyoneâsâmany peopleâs intuition is the opposite of that.â

These “all your RAM are belong to us” proclamations were delivered in-between sips of a slowly warming IPA (all the tech CEOs are now forced to discuss world historical moments while awkwardly smashing beers on podcasts), but will have far-reaching consequences if they actually come to pass. It’s not hard to imagine a future where everything is rented, not just movies and Google spreadsheets but also the AI models these companies hope will micromanage and ultimately monetize every spare moment of your life.

Being able to play Grand Theft Auto 6 locally once it gets ported to PC is a waste in the mind of Altman. Stream it from the cloud in-between datacenters burning tokens to scrape the web and replace it with AI-generated overviews instead. Better yet, have ChatGPT agents bid on your behalf against other agents for how much the spare compute is worth it to you to take a nightly drive around Vice City. Please clap.

#3792. Celeste and TowerFall dev explains why both games were suddenly delisted from Xbox

"We did this to support the BDS boycott."

Celeste and TowerFall have both been delisted from Xbox suddenly earlier this week. Per a post on Bluesky, developer Maddy Thorson says this was an intentional move, with the games being removed from sale on Xbox in support of the BDS (Boycott, Divestment, Sanctions) movement, which is aimed at protesting various companies linked to, or supporting, Israel's government during the genocide in Palestine.

"For those who're asking, yes we delisted Celeste and TowerFall on Xbox," states Thorson in a BlueSky post. "We did this to support the BDS boycott."

In case you're unaware, Xbox's inclusion on the BDS list is due to Microsoft's partnership with Israel and its prison system, according to BDS itself. The company has provided the country use of its Azure Cloud and AI systems, which have been used consistently over the past few years in the ongoing subjugation of Palestinians. BDS has urged people to cancel their Game Pass subscriptions, boycott leading Xbox franchises - including Call of Duty and Candy Crush - and cease purchases of Microsoft gaming products. As it stands, Celeste and TowerFall are now completely unavailable for purchase within the Xbox ecosystem.

This isn't the first time we've seen developers intentionally opt out of sales on Xbox because of the BDS movement; just a few weeks ago, Big Walk developer House House released a statement noting that its game is not on Xbox because of Microsoft's ties to Israel, and we saw the developer of Tenderfoot Tactics do the same in 2025.

"We would love for people to be able to play the game on Xbox, but not until Microsoft and/or Xbox have been removed as BDS boycott targets," noted the Australian developer at the time. "We've made this decision with the belief that meaningful change can be made in the world, that coordinated collective action can confront even the most powerful interests, and that one day, Palestine will be free."

Microsoft has responded to the BDS boycott previously, acknowledging that it supplied AI technology to Israel's Ministry of Defense, but claims "no evidence" it's been used to "target or harm people in the conflict in Gaza". Various reports, including the one linked above, refute this claim.

Celeste and TowerFall both remain available for purchase on PlayStation, PC, and Switch.

Selaco: The Machines of War arrives later this month.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

If you're a fan of first-person shooters and haven't played Selaco, you should. Built in the Doom engine and inspired by FEAR, Half-Life and System Shock, Selaco is a rollicking, dizzyingly ambitious sci-fi FPS where you battle a mercenary incursion of a vast, city-sized space station that's home to the last of humanity.

Launched into Steam early access in 2024, Selaco's first chapter alone is as long as some entire '90s shooters. Now, developer Altered Orbit Studios is preparing to release an update that will not only double the length of the game, but also introduce a wide array of new features and rework much of its existing design.

Described by Altered Orbit as "an absolute behemoth", Selaco: The Machines of War introduces the second of a planned three chapters to the FPS. Chapter two comprises 19 new campaign maps, which apparently amounts to "6-8 hours of additional content". Alongside further story elements and a voice for the protagonist, the chapter also introduces what sounds like a persistent enemy, in the form of "an unstoppable machine" that is "hunting you down."

Naturally, this second chapter also adds new weapons and enemies, with the former including a minigun and "a heavy machine gun that fires literal explosions". I don't know how that would work, but I'm keen to find out! Alongside your equipped arsenal, players will be able to use new deployable weapons like mini-turrets and sentinel drones, while the update also introduces a "heavy ordnance system" that lets you wield large, disposable weapons scattered across the battlefield, Gears of War-style.

As well as completely new stuff, Altered Orbit says the update will also enhance a lot of existing content. The FEAR inspired enemy AI, for example, has been "rewritten almost entirely from scratch" to facilitate smarter tactics and better decision making. The rewrite also introduces a new "rally" system and NPC area patrolling when not in combat—an addition designed to give players more agency in when and how fighting begins. Oh, and the entire first chapter has been given an overhaul that introduces "improved set pieces" and "new surprises".

And those are just the headline changes. Other improvements mentioned by Altered Orbit include a new lighting system, an overhauled particle system to make combat even more spectacular, improved navigation through Selaco's massive, mazey levels, new voice lines to make enemy communication even more lifelike, better controls, new music, and more. It almost sounds too good to be true, but I've played Chapter 1 and I know Altered Orbit can cook with rocket fuel, so none of this is beyond the studio's capability.

Selaco: The Machines of War arrives on November 13. The scale of the changes means that old saves will no longer be compatible. But if you don't fancy replaying the reworked first episode, you will be able to jump in at the outset of Chapter 2.

Celebrities wasted no time prepping for Halloween this year, as many have been showing off some truly slick costumes. Last year, Electra graced us with her Halloween spirit by dressing up as pinup model Bettie Page. This year, however, the actress and media personality showed off some growl power by dressing up as one of Batman's on-and-off love interests. Take a look at Electra's fit in the Instagram post below:

Meanwhile, Electra’s brand of humor has always been geared more toward sexuality, like wearing nothing but a slice of pizza and tomatoes in Meet the Spartans or bringing her sex appeal to parodying Scream Queens in the Scary Movie series. Still, I think Electra and Kat Dennings deserve some credit as well for having fun with the holiday. All in all, this is a holiday allows people to be anyone we want. So, whether it be a DC character or a vegetable, the sky is the limit!
