#3689. As “Black October” Comes to a Close, the Cybersecurity World Is on Edge

Read A Billion to One: From the mad scientists to the megadonors, a dispatch on the money, power, and influence of technology.

For months, the heads of frontier AI labs have been warning us that incidents like this summer’s Hugging Face hack could represent “early warning shots” before more menacing attacks in the years to come. Equipped with their own doomsday bunkers, some CEOs have begun instructing their teams to run preparedness scenarios for the day after a “catastrophic AI incident.”

“We are willing to accept some things going wrong,” OpenAI CEO Sam Altman told Vanity Fair’s global editorial director, Mark Guiducci, last month, adding that “there is a coming tidal wave of cybersecurity problems that are going to come from these open-source models.”

Just in time for spooky season, those warning shots got a little louder. On Wednesday, October 21, two serious security vulnerabilities were revealed in PHP, the programming language behind more than 70% of the internet’s web pages. Some cybersecurity professionals have already begun to call this “Black October,” thanks to the unprecedented spate of hacks across the globe.

AI did play a role in all this—but perhaps not the one you’d expect. Security researchers had actually used tools developed by OpenAI to discover the bugs months ago—and had been rushing to patch them up before they got into the hands of bad actors. Unfortunately, those vulnerabilities leaked last week, sending governments and businesses scrambling to protect their websites before hackers—perhaps armed with some of the very same AI tools as those defending against them—moved in.

Yet even the frontier labs’ ability to keep pace was called into question on Monday morning, when The Washington Post published a story about how Cathedral, a new cybersecurity company founded by four ex-DOGE staffers, successfully infiltrated some of Anthropic’s internal systems in just 12 hours. The article dropped just hours before Anthropic filed pre-IPO documentation detailing the potential risks to its own revenues and the world at large if its cybersecurity game were found to be lacking.

To the cybersecurity community, this was just the latest in a series of startling escalations. Joshua Achiam, who resigned from his post as OpenAI’s chief futurist this summer after nine years at the company, wrote on X: “Feels like March 1, 2020 for Cyber. Not normal, something is happening. Internet lockdowns in a couple of months?”

While these anxieties may not have reached your average American yet, business leaders have been growing increasingly concerned. In mid-September, executives from some of the world’s largest companies gathered for a special meeting of the Partnership for New York City. Their special guests that day were Anthropic whistleblower Jacob Coxon and former Department of Defense official Mark Beall, who had come to warn them about the threats posed by emerging AI capabilities.

The co-chairs, Pfizer CEO Albert Bourla and Tishman Speyer CEO Rob Speyer, looked out at their screens full of anxious CEOs from hedge funds and banks, as well as insurance, real estate, and pharmaceutical companies, and noted that it was one of their largest gatherings in years. One big topic on the minds of those gathered: AI-enabled cyberattacks.

During the Q&A portion of the talk, a representative from Coinbase raised his hand to ask what companies like his could do to combat the threat of “open-weight models in the hands of bad actors,” from cybercriminals to nation-states. (Coinbase CEO Brian Armstrong, meanwhile, has been one of the more outspoken advocates of deregulated, open-source AI.)

Earlier this month, Japan declared a “state of emergency” following sweeping cyberattacks on more than 20 major companies, from financial firms to rail operators. French authorities are still piecing together the mystery of how and why hackers targeted supermarket refrigerators around the country, spoiling millions of euros’ worth of food. Meanwhile, a new report from CrowdStrike suggests that recent attacks on South Korea’s financial sector were allegedly carried out by a single 26-year-old in China using an open-source AI tool.

Even here, cyberattacks have become so commonplace that you may have missed them in the flurry of headlines. (Did you catch this month’s massive breach of FBI employees’ personal details? Iran’s hit on more than 30 water systems in Minnesota this summer? And that’s to say nothing of mounting efforts by Russia to influence the midterm elections.)

I was surprised to learn that the concerns of most cybersecurity experts are both less apocalyptic and more present than the kinds of visions filling the heads of AI CEOs. In short, they believe that AI systems haven’t yet caused a paradigm shift in terms of the scale of damage they can inflict. What increased access to AI tools has done is lower the barrier to entry for even unskilled hackers to target low-hanging fruit.

“Over the coming weeks and months, the more likely scenario is a local hospital network in Ohio losing power and patients on life support dying as a result; a utility network in Texas taken offline; the lights going out across half of Wisconsin,” says Hamza Chaudhry, the AI and national security lead at the Future of Life Institute.

“We’re just in an exceptionally unresilient moment, coming up against systems which are designed to exploit that lack of resilience,” he tells me. “The largest providers,” however, “also have the most resources to defend themselves, including early access to frontier AI models for defense.”

He concedes that there is one more scenario that is keeping him up at night. “I’m very concerned about the so-called geopolitical Hugging Face moment.”

At the Munich Security Conference earlier this year, his group ran a simulation for an audience of national security officials from across the West: Imagine China develops a Mythos-level cyber-capability, which then gets into the hands of the mercenaries at the Wagner Group, who deploy it in Mali to target French military infrastructure. Then, much like in the Hugging Face incident, the agents go on an unintended side quest and attack mainland military infrastructure inside Europe. And that’s when things spiral out of control. “There was a real chance that Article 5 would be invoked and NATO would declare war on Russia” in this simulation, Chaudhry tells me.

A high-level executive at one of the world’s largest energy suppliers tells me he’s been losing sleep over aging infrastructure, budget cuts, and staffing shortages. Small utilities, he says, are plagued by “patches that might be easy to fix given the resources necessary.” But for now, “operators are running on Windows NT,” he says, referring to Microsoft’s 1990s operating system. New infrastructure coming online to support data center buildouts isn’t much better off. This infrastructure is “being built at such a speed [that] there’s no regulation and there are no hard standards,” says the energy executive. “Security is an afterthought, and that scares me a whole lot.”

This is the part of the story where I’d love to reassure you that the powers that be have been hard at work bolstering our defensive systems. The reality is, the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency has lost nearly a third of its workforce and hundreds of millions of dollars in funding, and it has failed to appoint an official director to lead the agency since the Trump administration took office in January of last year. But things at the state and local levels are what really worry the experts I spoke with. A recent Deloitte survey of state chief information security officers (CISOs) found that their budgets are failing to keep pace with growing threats—and have even faced cuts in 16% of the country.

“For some reason, amidst increasing cyber-capabilities, our defenders are running out of money,” Soham Mehta, a research fellow at the Foundation for American Innovation, tells me. “Great.”

There is at least some indication that authorities are beginning to wake up. Earlier this month, the new White House AI task force met for the first time to discuss cybersecurity and critical infrastructure protection, among other topics. Many are hopeful that frontier AI will do more to help companies and governments defend themselves than it will to help their attackers—as in the case of OpenAI’s assistance in discovering the PHP flaws. In a survey of more than a hundred national security officials last month, 81% said that defensive capabilities are very likely to improve with the help of AI.

None of the experts I spoke with advised me to load up the bug-out bag just yet. For now, our fate is largely in the hands of the government officials and executives who have to make the choice to invest in updated security systems.

They largely gave the same advice I’ve been working off for years. Set up a password manager, as well as two-factor authentication wherever it’s available. Beware of any unusual messages, and don’t drop your credit card details into any suspicious websites. And perhaps most importantly: Contact your local representatives to nudge them on updating that 1990s software.

#3688. 10 Hacks Every AllTrails User Should Know

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

AllTrails is a popular tool for finding walking, hiking, running, and biking routes around the world. You can use it to locate trails and check user reviews, but the app has plenty of features for customizing activities, tracking conditions, and navigating (safely) in real time. Here are the tips and tricks to get the most out of AllTrails.

The elevation map is useful for visualizing total gain and loss on your route, but you can scrub the chart on mobile to see exactly where climbs or obstacles are on the map. For example, you can see where the grade increases (and what the percentage is) or how far you are from stream crossings or switchbacks. Open the map from the trail page or the Navigate function and drag your finger across the elevation profile to track the location marker on the map.

You may be most likely to search for trails based on length and difficulty as well as location, but AllTrails has a wealth of filters to find routes with specific features, or that are dog- or kid-friendly. You can also use filters to identify trails that are likely to be less crowded (though if a route is on AllTrails, it certainly isn't a secret). In the Search window, tap All to open available filters. Select Not very busy under Visitation and Loop under Route type (out-and-back trails can feel busier). Select a rating and add any other requirements, then hit Show trails.

A free AllTrails account will get you most of the service's basic features, but you have to pay for a Plus subscription—$35.99 per year—for things like offline maps and wrong-turn alerts. If you have an REI membership, you get a 30% discount on paid AllTrails subscriptions, bringing the annual fee down to $24.99 per year. (A Peak subscription that usually costs $79.99 per year drops to $49.99 per year.) In the AllTrails app, go to your profile > Settings > REI Membership and follow the steps to connect your account and claim the discount.

User reviews can give you a good sense of current trail conditions, such as seasonal closures and whether there are muddy or snowy conditions, as well as more global environmental considerations like bugs and river crossings. You should obviously read the most recent reviews for your route, but you can also keyword search on desktop (CTRL/CMD + F) for terms like "mud," "scramble," "snow," "gate," "bugs," or "ticks." A trail may be marked as "easy," but this can reveal issues like snowmelt that have made running water trickier to wade through. You can read the reviews from the same month in previous years too.

When you search trails and trailheads by name on popular mapping apps, you may not always get directions to the exact starting location pinned on AllTrails. Instead, launch directions from the AllTrails listing to use the GPS coordinates, which you can then search in Google Maps or Apple Maps. On the trail page, scroll down to Get directions, then select your preferred map app (or copy the coordinates to the clipboard).

AllTrails maps have optional layers that contain a lot more data than just the route itself. All users have access to the Wildfire overlay, which shows current wildfire perimeters in the U.S. With a premium subscription, you get additional overlays for precipitation, temperature, ground conditions, snow depth, fall foliage, and community heat maps so you can see real-time environmental conditions at that specific location. A Peak subscription unlocks advanced overlays for slope angle, high-definition terrain, and public and private lands. Open a map and tap the Layers button in the upper-right corner.

Basic trail safety includes letting someone know exactly where you're going and when you plan to return. The AllTrails Live Share feature (available on paid plans) centralizes this information and shows trusted contacts where you are in real time so they can send help if things go wrong. When you share a link with safety contacts, they'll be able to see your real-time location, planned route, recorded mileage and elapsed time, estimated end time, coordinate info, and cell signal strength. They can also opt into SMS alerts. Activate Live Share under the Navigate tab—you'll need to generate a unique link each time you head out.

#3687. Lions' Jack Campbell Seemingly Unable to Move After Hit Against Vikings Player

Detroit Lions star linebacker Jack Campbell was seemingly unable to move following a tackle against a Minnesota Vikings player on Sunday, November 1.

Campbell, 26, was “immobilized,” according to FOX NFL commentators, following what appeared to be a relatively normal tackle against Vikings tight end T.J. Hockenson. He was moved onto a backboard and then a cart in order to be safely transported off the field after the Lions’ athletic training staff swarmed the linebacker, who did not move after his initial fall.

“This appears to be a serious scene in Detroit,” Michigan Sportscaster Brad Galli wrote via X after the tackle. “The Lions athletic training staff is moving with a purpose to help Jack Campbell, who fell and didn’t move.”

Shortly after, the official X account for the Lions shared an update on the linebacker’s status.

“Jack Campbell is being transported to a local hospital to be evaluated for a neck injury,” the post read. No additional updates regarding the player’s health status have been publicly revealed at the time of publication.

Several members of both the Vikings and the Lions were seen taking a knee for the duration of Campbell’s time on the field as an audible hush fell over the crowd at Ford Field in Detroit, Michigan.

Many of Campbell’s teammates — including edge rusher Aidan Hutchinson — were visibly upset after the play and while Campbell was tended to by medical staff. Several of Campbell’s teammates were seen wiping tears from their eyes as they tried to rally their fellow players after Campbell was removed from the field.

“Heavy emotions in Detroit,” Galli also wrote via X after his initial post regarding the incident. “All the Lions players and coaches surrounded Jack Campbell before he was carted off at Ford Field.”

Sideline reporter Erin Andrews spoke candidly about what Campbell means to the organization after speaking with a member of the team.

“He said, ‘This is Jack Campbell’s defense. I don’t hesitate to say that it goes through him and everyone in that locker room knows that,” Andrews, 48, reported on Sunday, seemingly also emotional as her voice cracked. “Point blank period.”

Legendary New England Patriots quarterback-turned-color commentator Tom Brady was asked how it’s even possible for teammates return to the field and the task at hand after watching what was clearly a severe injury.

“It’s very difficult for everybody, obviously, but it’s also part of what you’ve been doing your whole life,” Brady, 49, said on-air after Campbell was carted off the field. “He’s under great medical care and attention and you have to go back out there and do your job.”

The Lions ultimately defeated the Vikings 19-15.

#3686. Minecraft Creator Is Selling His $70 Million Beverly Hills Mansion, But There’s Something Unusual About It

Markus "Notch" Persson, the creator of Minecraft, is selling his Beverly Hills mansion that he bought back in 2014 for $70 million. At the time, Notch outbid Beyonce and Jay-Z for the home, and set a record for the highest price ever paid for a mansion in Beverly Hills.

He recently listed the home for the same price, despite the median Los Angeles home more than doubling in value over the past decade. Notch's 22,300-square-foot estate, however, is definitely a high-end property, and the market for such homes has cooled in recent times, The Los Angeles Times said.

Persson sold Minecraft to Microsoft in 2014 for $2.5 billion--the sale made Persson a billionaire due to his 70% ownership stake. A polarizing and controversial figure in gaming criticized for his remarks about LGBTQ issues and feminism, Persson had his name removed from Minecraft projects. Microsoft said his "comments and opinions" do not reflect those of Microsoft or developer Mojang.

Listing agent Aaron Kirma said Notch is selling because he doesn't spend much time in Los Angeles. Persson is also selling at a time when California's government and its billionaires have clashed over a proposed one-time 5% wealth tax on billionaires in the state. This measure is on the ballot for the upcoming elections on November 3.

Notch's home sits on about an acre in so-called "Billionaire's Row," featuring views of downtown Los Angeles and the Pacific Ocean. It has eight bedrooms and 15 bathrooms, as well as an elevator, pool, wine room, and a home theater. You can see photos of the space on Zillow.

#3684. Anthropic’s Pre-IPO Filing Is the Scariest Thing You’ll Read This Halloween Season

Read A Billion to One: From the mad scientists to the megadonors, a dispatch on the money, power, and influence of technology.

Just in time for the beginning of Halloween week, Anthropic dropped a 318-page filing for prospective investors considering joining its much-anticipated IPO in the coming days—a bone-chilling document no matter how you slice it. If you’re an AI skeptic in the vein of Ed Zitron, who believes the bubble’s well on its way to bursting, then the company’s reported loss of nearly $81 billion in the first half of 2026 will scare your socks off. Or maybe you’re an existential-risk doomer, in which case you’ll find plenty to be afraid of in the 97-page “Risk Factors” section, featuring totally normal investor warnings such as “sufficiently advanced AI systems could pose catastrophic or existential risks to society if not developed and deployed responsibly.”

Given that I’m somebody who’s covered these companies for a while, the number one question I get from friends and family these days is about what my concrete fears look like in a world overrun by AI. Increasingly, I’ve told them that a cyberattack of some significance is at the very least plausible in the coming year. (I can’t say that I found the cybersecurity section of Anthropic’s S-1 to be terribly reassuring.) And I was saying that before the cybersecurity community declared this month “Black October” thanks to the unprecedented wave of hacking activity, including attacks on French supermarkets and Japanese financial firms, and the accidental exposure of new vulnerabilities underpinning much of the internet.

Things got even more unsettling yesterday morning, when The Washington Post published a story about how Cathedral, a new cybersecurity company founded by four ex-DOGE staffers, successfully infiltrated some of Anthropic’s internal systems in just 12 hours. The article dropped just hours before Anthropic filed its pre-IPO documentation. Never one to pass up a good Lord of the Rings reference, Palantir CTO Shyam Sankar posted, “This is an undeclared emergency. You thought you were still inside the secure bastion of the king’s castle. You have awoken in Helm’s Deep. The orc armies are coming.” Others mocked all the melodrama. “Dawg they hacked [Anthropic’s] Slack lmao chill out,” posted the popular tech-world commentator Spor.

When it comes to those of us who aren’t stuck in the B-plot of Revenge of the Nerds, how much do we really have to worry about the safety of our information? I spent my week calling up cybersecurity experts to assess the actual risk level, where AI does and doesn’t play a role, and what you can actually do today to protect yourself from the next big hack.

Tough to know where to begin with former Yahoo CEO Marissa Mayer’s deeply tone-deaf interview with The New York Times about her new “AI wife” app, Dazzle. The part where Mayer is so stumped by having to come up with three nice bullet points to describe her daughter that she has to turn to AI? The part where she suggests gender inequality in tech isn’t a major issue? I’m not sure if Mayer is stuck in the #girlboss 2010s, but I do know none of this nonsense belongs in 2026.

The New York Times convened five experts—including New York State assemblyman Alex Bores, economist Tyler Cowen, and AI Now Institute policy lead Kate Brennan—spanning the full AI-safety spectrum for a roundtable about AI regulation. The frank discussion led to some fascinating exchanges between those who fear existential risk from the technology and those who suggest the whole thing is an overblown distraction from the real issues. Read on to see which participants went from quibbling over who’s a “useful idiot” to finding common ground over the fact that labs’ internal safety pledges are “not worth the paper they’re written on.”

Having already cribbed Reels from TikTok and Stories from Snapchat, Instagram is coming for a piece of YouTube’s long-form pie. The platform is beginning to roll out a new long-form, horizontal video format called Features, which will allow podcasters, comedians, and other creators to make videos up to 90 minutes long.

The real winners of the data center building bonanza? Suppliers of gray paint, apparently. According to a new feature in The New York Times, the paint company PPG has seen sales of its fireproof and rust-resistant gray paint triple in the last year. Also experiencing a surge in demand are purveyors of gravel, wires, and cables.

Status reports that some of CBS’s local election night coverage will be brought to you by DraftKings.

While Leading the Future raised more than $75 million after its founding last year, it seems the big money has dried up for the pro-AI group. According to NYT’s Teddy Schleifer, the super PAC reported no new donors in the first two weeks of October.

$6.6 million per employee: One of the bright spots to jump out of the Anthropic S-1 filing was the sizable revenue-per-employee amount, up from $1.4 million last year. I wonder how many newsletters I’d have to publish to rake in that kind of cash…

#3683. Love Is Blind's Jax Details What It Was Like Watching Season 11 With Ex Stew

Love Is Blind exes Jacqueline “Jax” Guelli and Scott “Stew” Stewart clearly have no bad blood after their brief, sight unseen engagement.

“I watched it with him,” Jax, 31, said on the Wednesday, October 28, episode of the “What’s The Reality” podcast, referring to her brutal breakup scene with Stew, 34. “Unfortunately, or fortunately, I got to be there with him when he saw what I said.”

Jax and Stew seemingly connected effortlessly inside the Love Is Blind season 11 pods, which was filmed in 2025 and began airing on Netflix last month. They got engaged sight unseen, only meeting face-to-face after Jax accepted Stew’s proposal.

Their engagement bliss, however, was short-lived. Moments after leaving the reveal tunnel, Jax stunned viewers when she brazenly admitted in a confessional that she wanted to leave the experiment without informing Stew.

“I had already seen it. I woke up at 3:00 a.m. to watch it,” she recalled to podcast host AD Smith of the premiere episodes. “It was even worse having him watch it with me, but at least … we were laughing a lot through the whole thing, at each other [and] at ourselves.”

She continued, “It was, like, actually really funny to us because we’re like, ‘Why did we say this? Why did we act like this? We’re coming off so douchy, like, all of this stuff.’”

Jax and Stew have remained friendly since ending their engagement.

“I think coming out of it, we both kind of know each other better and, you know, have remained close since,” Stew exclusively told Us in an October interview. “I would go so far as to say we’ve completely reconciled since then.”

He added, “You know, she reached out immediately after [and] kind of explained what was going through her head at the time. It didn’t have anything to do with me. It was just the situation, you know, and so … we’re good friends.”

Stew further hinted that Jax even kept hold of her much-discussed engagement ring.

“Word on the street is, if you catch her walking around Boston, she still has the ring,” he quipped, teasing, “You have to stay tuned to the reunion.”

Jax and Stew will reunite for the tell-all reunion, which hits Netflix Sunday, November 8.

“I think we’re going to talk about it more there, but, yeah, we hang out,” Jax noted on the podcast. “We live a block away from each other, so I see him in the neighborhood and doing errands. We bump into each other all the time!”

#3682. GTA 6’s Cops Will Send Dogs To Get You

The police in GTA 6 are smarter and more capable than they were in GTA 5, and that includes the newly confirmed detail that cops can dispatch dogs to hunt you down.

Edge Magazine recently posted a preview of the game with Rockstar's Rob Nelson playing. In one sequence, Jason and Lucia are attempting to evade police when they crash their motorcycle and try to escape on foot. However, nearby cops send out a K9 unit to assist. One of the dogs, a German Shepherd, quickly grabs Jason and pins him to the ground. According to Edge, developers standing by during the preview urged Nelson not to shoot the dog.

This implies that it's possible to shoot police dogs, and that wouldn't be surprising, as GTA 5 lets you shoot and kill dogs as well. We previously learned that players can pet the dog in GTA 6, or they can scold it.

In real life, police in Miami--which is parodied as Vice City in GTA 6--and other places around the country do indeed use specially trained dogs for crimefighting. Miami, in fact, just welcomed a new dog, Samson, who is also a German shepherd like the one in GTA 6.

GTA 6 features a six-star Wanted system and an expanded criminal profile system that allows cops to track you down with a wider net. Additionally, the game now notifies you if you've been seen by a CCTV camera, for example, and if so, you can destroy the evidence to evade the fuzz. Cops also remember the specific clothing that Jason and Lucia are wearing, so players may need to change clothes to escape.

In other dog-related GTA 6 news, the newest episode of South Park contained brand-new GTA 6 gameplay footage showing Jason hurling dog poop at another person, and then picking up the poop again to smack them with it.

GTA 6 launches on November 19 for PS5 and Xbox Series X|S. After that, Rockstar could release GTA 6 Online and a PC edition in early 2027.

#3681. This Powerful Lenovo Laptop Is Down to $629 at Walmart

If you’re shopping around for a reliable laptop but don’t want to spend an arm and a leg on a premium model from Apple, Lenovo has some highly underrated options that are versatile and offer great processor performance for the price—and it's now even more affordable, thanks to Walmart’s newly discounted Lenovo V14 G5 14-inch FHD Laptop, now 37% off and down to $629 (originally $999.99).

It’s powered by the 10-core Intel Core i7-13620H, with  six performance cores and four efficiency cores) and has a maximum turbo speed of 4.9GHz. It’s more powerful than many similarly priced 14-inch laptops and can excel at heavy multitasking, light video or photo editing, and data-heavy office work. It includes 16GB of DDR5 memory, comes with a 1TB PCIe 4.0 SSD for additional storage, and is powered by a modest 47Wh battery.

Despite its power, it’s relatively lightweight, clocking in at around three pounds and 0.7 inches thick. One reason the weight stays low is its plastic build. It might not feel as durable or premium as an aluminum laptop, but the tradeoff for an under-$650 price tag makes it worth it for those on a budget. The V14 G5 includes a range of ports, including two USB-A ports, one USB-C port, and an HDMI 1.4b port, as well as a headphone and microphone jack.

Still, if you’re looking for an everyday office or personal laptop with a strong processor, a solid port selection, and a lightweight build—but don’t mind a couple of cost-cutting compromises—the budget-friendly Lenovo V14 G5 14-inch FHD Laptop strikes the right balance between affordability and performance, especially at nearly $370 off.

#3680. “Knights Will Be Knights.” At Medieval Times, a Dinner-Theater Kingdom Faces a Reckoning

Once upon a time, on a boulevard carved into the dusty California flatland, there was a dethroned queen who gazed out upon her former kingdom. Erin Zapcic, 43, a Medieval Times monarch who reigned for 13 years before her dynasty crumbled, leaned against her 2016 Mazda 3 and studied the concrete castle across the road.

It was nearly midnight, and the subjects in paper crowns had already retreated home, bellies stuffed with butter-soaked corn, seared chicken shanks, and peppery tomato bisque slurped from pewter bowls. For $77.95 a ticket, the dinner-and-a-tournament show features a troupe of acrobatic performers in medieval garb who joust, trumpet, and brawl for dorky, drunk, or school-age patrons.

At Medieval Times, the 10 castles across North America draw an estimated 2.5 million guests annually to their two-hour feudal cosplay show.

In the grandiose main chambers of the Buena Park castle, beneath high-vaulted ceilings and self-referential decor, visitors drink beer from plastic souvenir goblets and queue to purchase light-up scepters and weaponry made of foam. Castle folk in tights and tunics address visitors as “my lord” or “my lady.” Some guests come in costumes of their own—velvet capes, lace-up bodices, and intricate braids.

Revelers are seated in tiered rows around a sand-filled arena and sorted by color, each section rooting for its knight. While “serfs” and “wenches” serve a four-course meal sans utensils, bellowing knights astride quarter horses compete in 11th-century games and rumble in choreographed hand-to-hand combat—a scripted mini drama in which one is crowned victor. The 10 castles across the realm of North America draw an estimated 2.5 million guests annually into a geeky fairy tale of feudal cosplay.

Actor Erin Zapcic as the queen at Medieval Times.

“When you work at Medieval Times, it becomes part of your identity,” says Zapcic, a petite brunette with arched eyebrows who now works as a business administrator. “And I’m struggling now because there’s a stupid little voice in my head going, ‘You’re not queen anymore.’” The glow of the chain restaurant’s LED sign cast her fair skin crimson. “I loved my job. But I couldn’t stand by while they mistreated us and the animals.” It had been her kingdom, after all, and she wanted it to be better. As problems bubbled up around her, she thought a union might force the company to answer for them.

Performers and union members protest outside Medieval Times Buena Park castle.

In 1381, England’s working class grabbed their pitchforks and rose against tyrannical landlords, extortionate taxes, and the stranglehold of serfdom. Six hundred and forty-one years later, Zapcic and her bearded counterpart, former knight Jake Bowman, led a ragtag group of performers to take a stand against working conditions and wages at the Buena Park castle.

It was an odd moment for a labor revolt: Medieval Times was enjoying a viral renaissance, its knights reborn as TikTok heartthrobs and its castles packed with guests who’d come to flirt with them. Behind the curtains, though, the work was less than chivalrous. According to a public filing before the National Labor Relations Board, pay for stable hands started around $16.75 an hour. Bowman and Zapcic say they were making $18.50 and $21.50, respectively, in a county where the median household income tops $100,000.

What began as a fight over wages would spiral into a year of upheaval: unionization drives at two castles, multiple lawsuits, claims of sexual harassment and animal abuse, and a nine-month strike. In the end, the union would be gone, and most of the people who built it were shunned, hazed, and scattered.

The story here—workers fed up with a company they say has wronged them—may sound familiar. In many ways, the Medieval Times crew could be a theater troupe, restaurant staff, or coed sports team. But this is no ordinary job, in no ordinary universe.

In this world, the cast—theater kids, high school athletes, and fantasy nerds—treats each performance as a live-action time machine to the Middle Ages. Wide-eyed children and tipsy fathers are spellbound by the playacting queens, unbearably luminous in their regalia. The knights are not just noblemen but athletes of the sand—flipping, flying, and growling into the arena. Like Fabio on a romance novel cover, they wear their hair long and grow out their beards.

At home, the fantasy lingers: Many of the performers have knight-themed Instagram and TikTok profiles (Jake Bowman once went by @sirjaketheknight), blurring whatever distinction remains between the role and the man. At what point do these personas stop getting hung up with the costumes at the end of the night? When does the fantasy run amok?

The Medieval Times story begins in Spain in the 1960s, when Jose Montaner converted his family’s farm into a barbecue restaurant, catering to Mallorca’s growing tourism industry. To compete with rival seaside attractions, he developed a medieval-themed indoor show that combined the immersive atmosphere of 1930s California-themed restaurants with the pageantry of English medieval fairs. Montaner had also seen El Cid, the 1961 Charlton Heston epic, and the film’s towers, period costumes, jousting, sword fights, and knights on horseback were all incorporated into the show.

The Montaners were nobility themselves: Jose’s mother was the Countess of Peralada, he claimed, and he held the rights to use the title of Viscount of Rocaberti. As Francisco Franco’s dictatorship waned and tourism surged, Montaner’s vision found success in Mallorca and Benidorm—and eventually crossed the Atlantic.

Funded largely by Spanish investors, the first US castle lowered its drawbridge in 1983, a $3.8 million gray-stone building, according to the Chicago Tribune, constructed about 15 minutes from Disney World in Orlando. Despite a tax-avoidance scandal with the IRS in 1996 involving the Florida and California castles, the Medieval Times brand grew, establishing 10 castles across North America by 2019.

Medieval Times stayed in the family: Jose’s son, Perico Montaner, eventually took over as president and CEO. Employees allege the company is run like a monarchy, with those at the top ruling with impunity. “The owners think they’re actual medieval lords,” says William Hainsworth, 58, a former Buena Park show cast manager. Neither Montaner nor Medieval Times responded to multiple requests for comment.

Fifteen years ago, in a swampy fiefdom on the opposite coast in New Jersey’s Meadowlands, Zapcic was a 27-year-old struggling actor who could not bear to wait another table. She took a job as a gift shop wench at the castle in Lyndhurst, New Jersey, a five-minute drive from her apartment, where she made $7.50 an hour to wear a corseted dress and hawk ceramic figurines and stuffed dragons. Though it paid poorly, it indulged her childhood fantasies and was the only job she had ever loved.

When she got the call to graduate from wenchdom and take the throne as a member of the cast, she was ecstatic. Years later, in 2018, Zapcic rode into the spotlight on a dapple-gray Andalusian, making Medieval Times history as one of the first-ever queens to ride in procession. She remembers tearing up as she descended through a dark tunnel into the thunder of a roaring crowd.

“Everything is really romanticized at the castle,” Bowman, a 37-year-old former knight with dark curly hair and a Bubba Gump Shrimp Co. T-shirt, says over hamburgers at Lazy Dog, a restaurant frequented by the Medieval Times cast.

Queen Erin Zapcic knights a VIP audience member backstage.

“Dude, the job is fun as hell,” he says. Getting paid to dress up, ride horses, and playact alongside long-haired hunks and red-lipped princesses? It’s not exactly a hard sell.

Some employees describe working at the castle as if it were a fantasy they dreamt up. Grown men clock in to work to wrestle in the sand with their friends, bond closely with their horses, and film thirst traps for social media on their lunch breaks. People date each other and party together. In interviews with Vanity Fair, former employees describe the environment as an intoxicating blend of performance adrenaline, late nights, and blurred boundaries—all charged with the sexual undercurrents of cosplaying in what could be a romantasy novel.

Knights ride on horseback during a Medieval Times performance.

Bowman says it seemed like the company knew that the job was fun. “And that’s what they’ll use to keep doing whatever they’re doing,” he adds. “My fairy tale popped when I broke my back.” Bowman fractured his lumbar spine after being kicked by a horse during his time at the Dallas castle.

In the arena, knights in polyester tabards battle for the queen’s favor, hurling, stabbing, and slamming each other to the ground. Though the combat is scripted and the punches are pulled, the toll on their bodies is real. “The job is a freaking grind,” Bryce Keizer, a former knight from the Buena Park castle, says from his car between deliveries at his new job as a process server. “It’s like a professional sport, but there’s no offseason.”

With a grueling schedule of 40 hours a week and two or three shows a day on weekends, the crew was perpetually run-down and exhausted.

Sidney Setzer, a former stable hand who quit due to exhaustion, says the physical demands of the job caused her to lose 35 pounds in 11 months. At the Buena Park stables, Zapcic estimates, about 30 horses were cared for by roughly 10 stable hands.

“The most serious injuries in equestrian care happen in the stalls,” says Purnell Thompson, who spent years working in the stables at the New Jersey castle. “You get bit, pinned, kicked.”

Purnell Thompson tends to a horse at Medieval Times.

In 2018, Hainsworth, who worked at Medieval Times on and off for 30 years, shattered his leg in front of 800 people. It was the first time he had broken character in his entire career, howling into his mic as children cried in the audience. In a lawsuit filed against Medieval Times in November 2024, Hainsworth alleged that shortly after the performance began, the horse panicked and slammed into the wall at roughly 35 miles per hour. “As a result, Mr. Hainsworth suffered severe injuries to his leg, necessitating emergency surgery a couple days later,” the lawsuit states. By 2024, he’d already had two surgeries and eight screws put in his knee. He walked with a cane and was preparing for a third surgery—a revision and knee replacement—six years after the first.

An X-ray shows Bill Hainsworth’s injured leg following an accident during a Medieval Times performance in 2018.

Hainsworth was fired in January of 2023 and alleged in the same lawsuit that he was wrongfully terminated in retaliation for reporting workplace safety hazards and requesting accommodations for injuries sustained on the job. Medieval Times did not respond to Vanity Fair’s questions about Hainsworth’s lawsuit, but has denied wrongdoing in court filings, saying it acted for “legitimate, non-retaliatory reasons” and provided reasonable accommodations; the case has since moved to arbitration.

“People get permanently injured and then aren’t able to work at Medieval Times anymore,” Bowman says. After his back injury, his mental health deteriorated so severely that he left the castle for several years before returning. “You have guys in their 20s with broken bodies,” says Zapcic, who suffered a hematoma after falling from a horse during a 2021 performance (an incident also mentioned in Hainsworth’s lawsuit). “And you’re not even getting paid what you’re worth.”

“I did not stay with Medieval Times for 30 years because I thought I was going to get rich,” Hainsworth says. In Orange County, where the median household income was $116,289 a year between 2020 and 2024, many castle workers earned barely above minimum wage when they began organizing in 2022. Stable hands qualified for food stamps; one squire was reportedly living in his car. “It’s hand-to-mouth with your pay, and for years you’re just surviving,” Zapcic explains. “The next thing you know, you’ve been there for 10 years, devoted your life and body to the castle, and you have no marketable skills to show for it.”

As legend has it, Sir Lancelot once crossed a bridge of swords to rescue Queen Guinevere, his hands cut to ribbons. In storybooks, knights are paragons of chivalry and honor. At Medieval Times, the knights are anything but that, says Angel Diamante. In 2016, Diamante was recruited from his neighborhood gym to audition for a knight position at the Buena Park castle, but as the only out gay knight in the locker room, he says he was appalled by the “unbelievable misogyny and homophobia” that was routine among the knights.

Knight Angel Diamante sits on a horse in the Medieval Times arena.

Knights across all 10 castles are an exclusively male order. In job postings, Medieval Times has stated that to “preserve the authenticity” of its theatrical production, knight roles are “reserved for male performers,” with the feeder role of squire likewise restricted. “The show takes place in medieval Spain, and yet we’re instructed to speak with English accents. The costumes have sequins; they sell frozen margaritas,” says Zapcic. “Authenticity is just whatever suits them.” Despite some documented examples of women participating in combat during the Middle Ages, no woman has ever worn armor in a Medieval Times arena.

“There’s like a whole pseudo-fraternity thing going on,” says former stable hand Thompson. Sean Quigley, a former Lyndhurst lord chancellor who shared the locker room with the knights, says “they would pull down their pants and wait for someone to come around the corner.” A former employee at the Scottsdale, Arizona, castle says that, as a new hire, he was hazed. He spent his first two weeks on the job running in the sand until he vomited instead of learning to ride. It was nearly a month into the role before he began dressage-style riding training.

Former employees say the energy in the locker room often carried into the rest of castle life. Instead of courtships, there was a steady churn of casual hookups among employees, where new female hires were treated like incoming freshmen, explains Zapcic. “You’re working long hours with people and then partying after,” she says. “Everybody dated everybody,” adds former queen Kate Farrell. “Things can get messy.”

Lexie-Lynn Taylor, a former queen at the Buena Park castle, says she experienced constant harassment from the knights’ department—especially from one knight. “He wouldn’t take no for an answer,” she recalls. Taylor describes inappropriate physical touch, as well as the knight cornering her and saying vulgar things.

Even when Taylor wasn’t being physically harassed, she says the atmosphere was punishing. “When I first started, I was talking to [a male coworker].” After sharing a kiss at the Christmas party, she says she felt slut-shamed and overheard members of the knights’ department referring to her as a “knight’s mattress” and “ye old whore.” “It went on for a month and a half before [he and I] just had to stop talking.”

Farrell says she also experienced harassment from a knight at the Buena Park castle. The knight offered to walk her to her car after a shift. “He pushed me up against my car and pressed his hand on my crotch,” she says. When he leaned in to kiss her, she slipped into her car and shut the door. They never spoke of it.

A former employee from Scottsdale says that in 2020, a female coworker filed a harassment report, which he corroborated as a witness. Rather than discipline the man, he says, the company moved him to another department with better pay. “On multiple occasions, I watched instances of poor behavior almost be rewarded,” he says.

There’s a “knights will be knights” attitude at the castle, says Quigley.

Knight actors perform a staged combat scene in the arena.

In the summer of 2018, Zapcic decamped for the western castle in Buena Park. California was a different kingdom entirely. She thought the riding lessons there were rudimentary and less fun, and that the head horse trainer, Franz Christian Garcia, was hostile.

One afternoon when lessons had been moved to the outdoor turnout, Zapcic felt her horse creeping up on her shoulder when the rule was that the horse never leads. The correction, Garcia had taught her, was to hit the animal in the face with the reins. She had never liked doing it, she says, and she did it lightly. Afterward, Garcia pulled her aside. “What you did was correct,” she remembers him saying, “but don’t do it when you’re outside of the castle because people are driving by and they might see it and think it’s abuse.”

“It made me question,” she says, “if somebody sees what we’re doing and will think it’s abuse, why is that the way that we’re training the horses?” It was the first red flag she saw in the stables.

In June 2019, Bethany Regan, a former cast member at Buena Park, filed a lawsuit against the company alleging that Garcia was “whipping the horses unnecessarily and to the point where one of the horses had large welts over its body,” in addition to causing the animals to suffer dehydration, mouth bleeding, and exhaustion. Regan’s complaint mentions the allegation that the treatment of the animals “not only led to the injuries to the horses, but also [resulted] in the death of a horse.”

The suit also alleges that Regan reported “the mistreatment of and cruelty to the horses” to her managers (and to California’s Occupational Safety and Health Administration), and that the company then suspended her for what it called “starting rumors” and fired her in March 2018. According to Regan’s filing, she had recently been promoted, had been named employee of the month, and had never received a written warning about her work.

The case settled out of court in 2020. Medieval Times, Regan, nor Garcia responded to Vanity Fair’s request for comment.

Concerns like Regan’s have also drawn scrutiny from animal welfare groups. PETA says they receive “a couple of dozen” complaints each year alleging that the animals used in the show exhibit “signs of severe stress.” “Horses are notoriously skittish animals,” a PETA spokesperson tells Vanity Fair. “Medieval Times subjects them to loud music and strobe lights, and forces them to engage in raucous activities…sometimes under the threat of a whip.”

Just before the 2024 Paris Olympics, six-time Olympic medalist Charlotte Dujardin was suspended for a year by the International Federation for Equestrian Sports after a video showed her whipping a horse repeatedly during training. (Dujardin has since said she is “deeply ashamed” and that the incident “does not reflect how [she] trains [her] horses or coaches [her] pupils.”) Zapcic says that if a horse can feel a fly land on its rump, a light cue is more than enough, and there’s rarely, if ever, a need for force.

But inside the Buena Park stables, Setzer says, restraint was not the rule. “There were no limits on how hard the trainers could go on the horses,” the former stable hand explains. “The horses would come back with visible raised welts on their hindquarters from whipping.” According to Setzer, during training sessions, the trainer would tie either side of a horse’s face and whip its back legs until the animal became so stressed it jumped straight into the air. Like Regan, Setzer says she reported the abuse to management and they “brushed it off.” Neither Medieval Times nor Garcia responded to requests for comment about these allegations.

In September 2022, Brandon Sanchez, a member of the show cast, documented a riding lesson in an email to management and HR, describing Garcia berating riders and whipping a Friesian horse for an extended period. Sanchez wrote that the horse was run so hard it “slid down into the sand with his front legs curled up beneath him,” was “drenched with sweat,” and appeared “extremely uncomfortable,” adding that the incident “disturbed [him].” He described it as the only time he witnessed a horse being treated that way. After his email, Sanchez described subsequent lessons with Garcia as just “walking in circles with little instruction.”

In April 2023, Garcia served Bowman with a defamation lawsuit after Bowman posted a video to X, in a since-deleted thread, showing Garcia appearing to beat a horse during a training session. Appended to the end of the video were still photographs of injured horses, taken by Setzer during her time in the stables, she confirmed to Vanity Fair. In the suit, Garcia alleged the video was “false and misleading.” The suit states that in the video Garcia “can be seen employing appropriate training techniques with the horses, including by using a lunging whip to maintain the animals’ focus,” and while the whips “create a loud popping noise, they did not injure the horses.” The horse in the video, the suit reads, “was an entirely different horse than the one shown in the photographs with injuries.”

Garcia has consistently denied abusing the horses and maintains that Bowman’s post misrepresented the footage and context. The case was dismissed in April 2025. Garcia continues to work as the head horse trainer at the Buena Park castle. Bowman declined to comment on the case; Garcia did not respond to a request for comment.

Kate Farrell, a former performer who played a queen, holds a protest sign outside Medieval Times in Buena Park, California.

The job that so many had described as the best of their lives was, by 2022, springing leaks—in the arena, in the locker room, and in the stables. For a handful of castle folk, the answer was to organize. In late June 2022, the Lyndhurst castle announced it was filing for an election to unionize—which, if successful, would be the first union in Medieval Times history. As lore has it, the Lyndhurst castle tried to unionize in 2006, to great disappointment. More than 15 years would pass before anyone tried again.

When Zapcic and Bowman heard about the union effort in New Jersey, they knew they had to move quickly. “With a union contract, a code of conduct is established,” says Zapcic, “for the care of the horses, for how harassment allegations are investigated, for disciplining misconduct, and for holding management accountable.” This was their answer.

Within five days, the duo, operating out of a Starbucks across the street, had secured the signatures needed to file for their own election in California. Medieval Times hired a $3,200-a-day anti-union consultant, according to a federal labor disclosure filing. It even sued the newborn union, then operating as Medieval Times Performers United, for using the company’s name and logo—a move so aggressive that not even Amazon and Trader Joe’s had tried. (Trader Joe’s would go on to sue its own union over trademark in 2023.)

In November 2022, Buena Park won its election by nine votes and was certified, joining Lyndhurst under the American Guild of Variety Artists (AGVA), the national union for live variety entertainers. But the battle was just beginning for the two castles.

A person protests outside Medieval Times in Buena Park, California, 2023.

A Medieval Times performer dressed as a knight holds a sign during a strike in 2023.

After four stalemated bargaining meetings on February 11, 2023, the Buena Park union went on strike, slipping out one by one before the second show of the day. There was a big turnout: local representatives, labor groups, and media outlets—all armed with megaphones and printed signs—walked alongside Zapcic and her fellow union members. “Guests were turning around and not going in,” Kate Farrell remembers. “It was really powerful.”

The feeling was short-lived. Shortly after the walkout, the company flew in performers from other castles to replace its striking workers, according to former employees.

“Every single day for nine months, thousands of people crossed our picket line and called us assholes in the name of a two-hour show,” says Zapcic. “We even printed photos of the abuse—horses bleeding, with big welts and whip marks,” says Setzer. “And parents would just cover their children’s eyes and walk inside.” On one April night outside the castle, several picketers were struck by a patron’s car, and a few others were shoved by the passenger who got out of the vehicle, according to video footage later aired by Fox 11 Los Angeles.

Taylor was outspoken about her reservations about unionizing. Caught off guard by the walkout and without other work lined up, she crossed the picket line—and continued to do so for weeks—entering through a back entrance to avoid hostile strikers. “They were trying to hurt the company by walking out, but they ended up hurting the people they called their friends,” says Taylor.

As the divide between union members and Medieval Times loyalists deepened, anonymous troll accounts surfaced and began posting content harassing those on the picket line. One Instagram account, @scabbydoo316, targeted female picketers. In posts and comments seen by Vanity Fair, the account referred to the striking queens Julia McCurdie and Kate Farrell as “bicycles”—an innuendo used to imply the women had been repeatedly “ridden.” “The worst part,” McCurdie says, “was seeing people I worked with and had close relationships with ‘liking’ and commenting on those posts.”

Performers and supporters chant and hold signs during a protest outside Medieval Times in Buena Park, California, 2023.

Taylor admits she was part of that world for a while. “A few [people] felt very validated by Scabby attacking the strikers under the guise of standing up for the little guys who stayed,” she says. She was in contact with the person running the account, who often sent her drafts of videos and memes before posting them. Looking back, she says she regrets how swept up she got in the feud.

As the harassment continued and the months slogged on, strikers couldn’t afford the battle, and many had to find other work. “It was a slow trudge toward defeat,” says former Buena Park performer Graham Wojcik. Each day, fewer people responded in the group chat, and the ranks thinned. “I struck by myself multiple times,” says Bowman. As November 2023 approached, nearly a year since the election, the union was in danger of losing its certification. Picketers had to hang up their signs and face the reality of returning to the castle.

The returning employees said they found the transition back to work far more difficult than they had expected. “They never had any intention of us coming back. They had replaced us,” says McCurdie. “The amount we were relentlessly harassed and retaliated against by our coworkers was awful,” says Zapcic.

Bowman says that some knights even warned returning strikers that there would be consequences for having left. “There’s a lot of moments in the choreography where [a fellow knight] can hurt you. It’s designed for the person to have restraint,” he says. “I was concerned for my safety.”

Bowman never got the chance to find out what awaited him inside the castle. When the striking workers returned to their posts in November 2023, he and two other union members were refused reinstatement for “misconduct during the strike.” He believes it was over a crude drawing of a manager he’d made and carried on the picket line.

“On our first day back, we had to do mandatory harassment training,” says Farrell. “Here I was, watching this video about things they had been doing to me for months. It was crazy.”

“We were told it was a privilege to clean horse stalls,” Keizer, who quit two days after returning from the strike, remembers. According to Farrell and Zapcic, former kings and queens were instructed to spend hours a day doing vocal exercises. “We would stand in a circle and say ‘Jake the jailbird jacked the jeep’ over and over,” says Farrell. “We all knew they were just dragging it out to make sure we never performed again.”

“Three months after we returned, the knights still hadn’t ridden their horses or performed in a show,” says Zapcic.

Farrell reported the online harassment she faced on the picket line to management. The company’s attorneys, she says, dismissed the posts as “protected anti-union activity” and declined to investigate. She left Medieval Times in 2024 and now performs at another castle, in a popular theme park down the freeway.

In May 2026, Farrell filed a lawsuit against Medieval Times, alleging sexual harassment, retaliation, and gender discrimination. Among the claims: that after she reported the harassment, a manager retaliated by having a subordinate remove the stitching from her costumes to cause “wardrobe malfunctions in front of live audiences.” She was then restricted, according to the suit, to a single matinee whose script condemns cyberbullying, forcing her “to perform lines about the harm of malicious rumors while her own harassment went unaddressed.” Medieval Times has denied wrongdoing, saying in a June 2026 filing that it took “all reasonable steps to prevent discrimination” and asking that the case be dismissed. The case is currently pending in California state court.

Despite the strike, the Buena Park union never won a contract. Thousands in the hole and out of options, says Zapcic, AGVA, the performers’ union, finally stepped away after workers, backed by the National Right to Work Foundation, filed to decertify at both castles. The day AGVA’s withdrawal notice reached corporate, Zapcic quit. Her final show was on February 13, 2024—her 13th anniversary at the company. “It was my time to get out,” she says.

Queen Erin Zapcic holds a rose on her final day at Medieval Times.

And so, they did not all live happily ever after. For those who fought, the story dragged on.

On a humid March evening in 2025, Erin Zapcic sipped Sauvignon Blanc in an Irish bar four miles from the castle where her Medieval Times career began. She was in town from California, visiting family in New Jersey, and invited some friends from her Lyndhurst days for a reunion. About a dozen castle alumni of varying ages mingled over fried mozzarella sticks and mustard-covered pretzels. There were a few balloons.

Weeks earlier, a National Labor Relations Board judge ruled that Medieval Times had violated federal labor law in its efforts to defeat the union campaign. The company has appealed, challenging some of the judge’s findings and arguing that the judge lacked authority to issue the decision. Medieval Times and Montaner did not respond to requests for comment on the case.

It was 6:30 p.m., which meant that just 10 minutes down Route 17, a queen was applying a final coat of red lipstick, adjusting her crown, and mic’ing up. Horses were whinnying in the stalls. Hundreds of guests stood in line outside, abuzz with anticipation while servers rushed to prepare hundreds of roast chickens. A bit later, a shaggy-haired knight would win the final competition, beat his chest, and throw a triumphant fist in the air as his section screamed for him.

Back at the pub, the mood swung between cheery “remember whens” and indignation, almost two years of defeat still hanging in the room. “You can look back on something as the best time in your life and also recognize that it was extremely toxic,” says Zapcic. “But because of them, I’ll always be a queen.”

Queen Erin Zapcic waves to the audience on horseback during her final performance at Medieval Times.

#3679. Phantom Blade Zero Is Already Proving Its Prelaunch Hype Was No Fluke

Just a few hours into launch, Phantom Blade Zero is already a hit game on PC. There was considerable hype behind the game as it was estimated that it had sold 1 million units before launch, and at the time of writing, it has peaked on Steam with 723,876 concurrent players. That's an impressive start for the game, and considering that it's also available on PS5, it's likely that quite a few people are enjoying its mix of soulslike-adjacent action, fight scenes choreographed by movie legend Donnie Yen, and a setting inspired by Chinese folklore.

Alinea Analytics' Rhys Elliott gave a breakdown of those preorder sales--when they had reached 850,000 units sold--explaining that 62.5% of Phantom Blade Zero's pre-launch sales came from China, Taiwan, and Hong Kong. "These markets--but predominantly China--account for 75.9% of the copies on Steam and about 24.9% on PS5," Elliott wrote, noting that the early sales had generated $43 million in revenue.

In a launch-day letter, creative director Soulframe Liang thanked the fans for Phantom Blade Zero's strong start, and the people in his studio, S-Game, for bringing his vision to life. "This is a game of immense scale, made with all the passion in our hearts. It is a gift from a small group of gamers who just happen to be developers, to every gamer who shares our love for gaming," Liang wrote.

Phantom Blade Zero is off to a strong start, but it doesn't quite look like it'll be a repeat of another hit game from the Chinese game development scene, Black Myth: Wukong. That game managed to sell an astonishing 10 million units in just its first three days, and while Phantom Blade Zero probably won't reach that same figure, it's still in the top 40 games of 2026 by revenue, according to Elliott--not too shabby considering just how packed 2026 has been with new releases.

If you're looking to get started, you can check out our Phantom Blade Zero guides hub for many walkthroughs on increasing your power and finding rare items. "S-Game's Wuxia-inspired combat puts you in the middle of a Chinese action movie," Richard Wakeling wrote in GameSpot's Phantom Blade Zero review.

There’s no denying that The Hunger Games films are some of Jennifer Lawrence’s best movies. Fans get to see her play the strong yet complex Katniss Everdeen, who volunteers to take her little sister’s place in a deadly, televised game show. While critics and audiences have long raved about Lawrence’s performance in the movie, her own mother had a savage take (and I was shook to learn about it).

Jennifer Lawrence’s performance as the District 12 tribute truly was groundbreaking for female action characters. In fact, Maya Hawke, who's playing a young Wiress in its film series' prequel, Sunrise on the Reaping, spoke highly of Lawrence impacting the action genre. But, even with all of the praise the Oscar winner gets, Lawrence revealed on Call Her Daddy that her mother mainly noticed one thing while watching her on the big screen:

My mom, at the premiere of The Hunger Games, said she could tell in every scene when I had my period. Water retention, I guess. Imagine a day of me being on camera that that doesn't go through my mind.

Wow, talk about embarrassing! I never could have imagined how savage Mrs. Lawrence could be in her critiques. I suppose, if anything, it proves she clearly knows her own daughter very well. Also, just for the sake of transparency, I certainly wouldn’t have been able to tell the Silver Linings Playbook actress was on her period in specific scenes.

Then again, I also had no idea Lawrence was on Ambien while filming the dancing scene she had with Plutarch in Catching Fire. And I imagine I also wasn't the only one who didn't know she surprisingly peed on the set of the first film. As wild as her mom's critique is, I’m curious as to which scenes led the matriarch to her brutally honest assessment.

Jennifer Lawrence’s mother may have had a bone to pick with her daughter’s Hunger Games performance, but it doesn’t mean she’s not a fan of the talented actress’s work as a whole. Lawrence had a lot of kind words to share about her mama, and they sound so relatable:

She's also like the most supportive and the person I'm so excited to tell exciting news to. I don't know if I think all moms do this where you're like, ‘Guess what?’ And they just say the most out like the craziest, like it will never live up to it, you know? I'm like, ‘Guess what?’ And she's like, ‘Oh my god, you wrote a movie. You're winning an Oscar for best writer, director, and you're acting in it and just won an Oscar for that.’ And I'm like, ‘No.’

It's definitely on brand for a mother to overestimate her daughter’s good news! But it’s sweet to know that Lawrence has such a supportive mother that she can always come to when good things happen for her.

What I think this all speaks to is how parents can still keep us on our toes, no matter how old we get. And, in the case of Jennifer Lawrence, she's gone on to do exceptional work since the original Hunger Games series ended. I just wouldn't expect her to rewatch the films with her mom any time soon.

You can continue to give praise to the award-winning star by watching The Hunger Games movies with a Hulu subscription. You can also make sure to check out the 2026 movie release Sunrise on the Reaping, which hits theaters on November 20th and features Lawrence reprising Katniss.

Just your average South Floridian cinephile who believes the pen is mightier than the sword.

#3676. Taylor Swift Skips Kansas City Chiefs' Game Against Denver Broncos

Taylor Swift apparently decided to turn down the opportunity to get a little Mile High as the Kansas City Chiefs faced off against the Denver Broncos.

The pop star, 36, did not appear to be in attendance for the Chiefs’ Sunday, November 1, AFC West showdown against the Broncos at Empower Field.

Swift’s apparent absence continued her recent trend of not traveling with husband Travis Kelce and the team for road games. Instead, the pop star appeared to spend the day at a FYC screening of Toy Story 5 alongside the beloved animated film’s director Andrew Stanton.

“Yeah, so I was on a tour that was, um, a lot of things but it was pretty physically exhausting and it was a 3-and-1/2 hour show and one of those tours — I have actually never experienced this level of exhaustion between shows,” Swift recalled of her history-making Eras Tour and how her brother, Austin Swift, convinced her to lend her voice to the film’s soundtrack. “I was like in bed all the days that I wasn’t playing a show just trying to rest up.”

She continued, via social media footage, “So my brother contacts me … sometimes we talk like siblings and sometime we have business conversations that are half-business, half-siblings … he calls me up and he’s like, ‘Hey, I really think you need to see Toy Story 5.'”

Safe to say, Swift’s calendar remains full as her husband experiences what is said to be his last season in the NFL.

Earlier this week, Kelce, 37, responded after Prince William jokingly said he tried bumping the Chiefs star out of a selfie he took with Swift at an Eras Tour stop in England in 2024.

“I get it, man,” Kelce said on the Wednesday, October 28, episode of his “New Heights” podcast. “I was just a boyfriend at that point, you know? I wasn’t her husband yet, you know.”

Kelce joked that the Prince, 44, was likely thinking, “’We don’t really know if this is going to last, so [can you] just move out of the way real quick so we can keep this photo forever?’”

Swift and Kelce got married in July at New York City’s Madison Square Garden.

Since tying the knot, Swift has appeared at every Chiefs home game at Arrowhead Stadium. She last attended Kansas City’s 22-6 win over the Los Angeles Chargers on October 18. At that game, beauty influencer Ashlie Molstad described the scene when Swift took her throne inside her suite during the first quarter.

“Three big ass dudes come in and they are there for security for Taylor,” Moldstad explained. “Then you just kind of start observing what the f*** is going on and what that world is like. [The security team] is head on a swivel as if they’re Secret Service, right? I mean, she is the most famous, at least American, celebrity that we have right.”

She continued, “Anyway, there’s these three men and they’re very friendly to us. They’re very nice. But they are very locked into…they are not watching the game. They’re watching people. It was kind of wild to see how many people are constantly looking.”

The Chiefs return home for their next game, hosting the New York Jets on Sunday, October 8.

#3675. Xbox’s Recent Efforts Haven’t Changed Anything And The Future Remains Bleak, Expert Says

Xbox CEO Asha Sharma has undertaken a number of efforts thus far to help get the business back into a healthy place, and nothing has worked, Circana analyst Mat Piscatella says.

He told The Game Business that based on the sales and engagement data he sees for the US gaming industry, "I'm not seeing [the moves] have any positive impact" for Xbox.

The disc-to-digital program "hasn't changed their sales of new physical software trend at all," he added. Additionally, making Gears of War: E-Day exclusive on console to Xbox "hasn't made any difference" in terms of selling more Xbox hardware. In fact, Xbox sales continue to spiral. Sharma says there is a supply issue, but, in the US at least, you can get a new Xbox very easily.

Piscatella said E-Day is a "Gears-ass Gears of War game," and a gorgeous one. But making it exclusive to Xbox created a scenario where "you chop the legs out" from under its potential potential to boost Xbox generally. "At least in the short term, it hasn't made a difference," he said.

There was clear and obvious evidence that E-Day was planned for PS5, but it was never released on Sony's console. Other industry experts said Microsoft purposefully sent E-Day out to die "for hearts and minds."

Additionally, Piscatella said Sharma's decision to remove new Call of Duty games from Game Pass was another loser of a decision. He said the data he's seeing shows that the Call of Duty franchise "lost a ton of engagement" due to Modern Warfare 4 being stripped out of Game Pass.

"And you got no benefit. It’s really hard to find any signs of positivity or hope on that platform right now," he said.

Piscatella went on to say that the efforts Microsoft is undertaking are for "Twitter likes" from hardcore fans. "But other than that, in terms of actual results, I'm not seeing anything right now," he said.

Sharma's turnaround plan for Xbox was never expected to yield immediate results--she only took the job in February and she inherited numerous foundational problems. In a memo to staff seen by CNBC, Sharma said she's taking a "long-term" view to help turn things around, and that includes pushing every studio to return to growth for players and revenue by the end of the fiscal year ending June 2027. Beyond games, Sharma has established a unit called XP, which will expand Xbox's games across film, TV, consumer products, sponsorships, and live experiences, as well as new initiatives in China.

Also in the memo, Sharma said she will push her teams to help Xbox get back in line with rivals Sony and Nintendo by 2027 in terms of profit margins, and then beat them by mid-2030. For comparison, Xbox currently reports about a 3% internal margin, which compares to 9.9% for PlayStation and 16% for Nintendo, according to CNBC.

A 3% profit margin means that for every $100 that Xbox brings in, it spent $97 to do so and keeps $3. A higher profit margin is better, and that's what Sharma is pushing for.

#3674. Creativity Is Conning Us

We are culturally obsessed with innovation. Consider TED Talks and Apple’s “Think Different” campaign and our obsession with tech founder-philosophers. The writer Thomas Frank has. In The Creativity Con: How Innovation Became America’s Biggest Racket, the author deconstructs what he calls “our national fascination with creativity.” The book has chapters on neoliberalism, AI, and the current concept of the creative class. His research included a long trip to a music festival turned marketing love-in, South by Southwest, which he describes in his smart, dry way as a “marathon trade show with something like 40,000 attendees” and “a more inclusive, more lovable version of Davos.”

Frank, who is 61 and lives in Maryland, is best known for his bestselling books about politics, including What’s the Matter With Kansas? and Listen, Liberal. But his new book is in some ways a belated sequel to his first book, 1997’s The Conquest of Cool, about how advertising co-opted the rhetoric of the 1960s counterculture to sell us Pepsi and cars. (It’s the kind of book you’ll think of often: anytime you see the launch of a new extreme energy drink and still required reading for anyone doing a Mad Men rewatch.)

Since Frank’s newest work focuses on creativity and innovation as the drivers of American affluence, I thought meeting him on his book tour for slop bowls at Sweetgreen, a salad marketed as an efficient and innovative way to get a nutritious meal, would be apropos. But the Sweetgreen on the Upper East Side was both loud and had nowhere to sit, a sad reflection of how Americans view workday lunches. Luckily, a small Vietnamese restaurant on Lexington Avenue became a welcome space for bahn mi and a discussion of the great man theory, the midterm elections, and using AI for gardening advice.

This interview has been condensed for length and clarity.

Vanity Fair: I can’t believe you were at South by Southwest for nine whole days researching this book.

Thomas Frank: Longer. It goes for 10 days, and I was determined to see the whole thing.

Did it make you depressed, or what was your takeaway?

Well, I was fascinated. That was one of the first things I did for the book. It was March of ’23. So, you know, I—I had my theories and my ideas and my preconceived notions, and I was like, “What? What am I going to find?” I wasn’t prepared at all for what swept over me.

One of my favorite parts of the whole book is that the CIA was there at the Creative Industries Expo.

I love that when they asked you if you had any questions you asked them a spicy question about the JFK assassination. What else did you do early on for research?

I went back and read [Thomas] Carlyle, On Heroes, Hero-Worship, and the Heroic in History. That is where he introduced the great man theory of history. He thinks the nature of humanity is to worship heroes, and that sort of gave rise to this sort of whole genius theory. So I didn’t talk about any of this in the book—it all got left on the cutting room floor—but then in the 19th century, they had this theory of the great genius, that Franz Liszt or Napoleon or Goethe had this spark and we had to sort of honor them. And they were quasi-magical, because we couldn’t really understand how they did it. And that obviously rubs Americans the wrong way. Even though our democracy is falling to pieces, we are an intensely egalitarian people.

How did you decide what to cover and keep in the book?

The way I decided to do the book was historical and then sociological. So I did the historical part, and a lot of it is [about] Obama and Reagan. And then for the sociological part, I decided I would choose a state and describe the innovation initiatives there. And I chose Maryland because I live there. I chose an industry, and the one I chose is the defense contractors.

Defense contractors love to talk about how innovative they are. There are like five industries that really abuse this language [of innovation]: defense, advertising, pharma, the tech guys, and Wall Street.

What is the creepiest thing you learned about defense contractors?

The contrast between what they make and the way they describe it, which is wholesome all-American innovation. It’s language that’s just camouflage.

You’ve written a lot about politics. Do you think there’s going to be a big midterm shift happening?

The country is definitely turning against Trump. But then again, what do I know? The polls have been so wrong all these years. I mean look, the Iran war is so unpopular, and it’s really unpopular with the very people that voted for him.

They have to have something that they stand for, and it can’t be innovation.

Oh yeah, absolutely. The Republicans used to love the language of creativity, and the Democrats liked the language of innovation. So [President] Carter used to talk about innovation all the time, and at the same time, Reagan was always talking about creativity. Nobody said at the time, “this is a battle between innovation and creativity.”

How do you define the difference between innovation and creativity?

Technically, innovation has to do with actually producing a product. Creativity means facility with art and language. But in practice, the words overlap all the time and are used as synonyms. They were basically synonyms and then split back in the ’60s when creativity was identified with the counterculture, and innovation was identified with engineers, military, industrial, and technology. And the counterculture really turned against all of that stuff.

It’s funny that after all of your political books, this one still ends with Trump.

Yeah, Trump and AI. The last chapter is all about it.

I have no technical understanding of it, so I wouldn’t know. I don’t think anybody else knows either because it’s all private. It’s proprietary. I compare it to a private sector Manhattan project. My wife is an economist. She finds it extremely useful. In my work for this book, it was not useful.

I’m really into gardening, and it’s very helpful with gardening. It’s very helpful with household chores. It knows a lot about stereo equipment.
