#3673. How I'm Using the Time Change to Kickstart My Morning Exercise Routine

I look forward to the fall time change every year, because I have plans for that extra morning hour. Turning back the clock is a perfect opportunity to kick-start a morning routine, since you can get up an hour early without it feeling like you're getting up an hour early.

We are, unfortunately, still doing clock changes twice a year. But I will take advantage of that fact while I can, because the fall time change gifts us with an extra hour in the morning, even if it is cruelly ripped from our evening routines. I'm not a morning person by nature, but my day always goes better when I get my workout in early, so I'm going to take that extra morning hour and use it for a workout instead of recalibrating my body clock to wake up later. I recommend all my fellow night owls do the same.

I mean, you could use your extra hour to sleep in—take it if you need it. But personally, I'm going to set my alarm an hour earlier than I get up, starting on Nov. 1, the first day of standard time for 2026. An hour is enough time for a simple strength workout or for a short run and a quick shower before officially starting your day. I reserve one day a week for sleeping in, which for me is Saturday. On days I'm resting from exercise, I'll still wake up on schedule but use my morning hour for something fun or relaxing, like reading a book.

If you want to fit a full workout in and need more time than the hour gives you, this is still a good way to soften the blow. For example, you can wake up 90 minutes earlier (according to the clock) with it only feeling 30 minutes earlier than usual (according to your circadian rhythms). I've been using my extra hour a little differently each year, depending on how committed I am to those morning workouts. This year, I may split it between extra sleep and a mini workout.

On the first day you wake up "early," things will be much as they always are. But now that you're becoming a morning exerciser, you'll have to come to terms with the winter darkness. It will creep in, sunrise getting a few minutes later each day, until your morning jog is, most likely, fully in the dark.

If you are running in the early mornings, definitely get yourself a light to help you see and be seen. I have a Petzl Tikkina, which I bought a few years back because Petzl has a reputation for reliability, and the Tikkina is one of their more affordable models. It's worked so well that the second winter I used it, I sprang for the rechargeable battery that fits in place of its three AAA cells. The rechargeable is designed to work well even in cold conditions, which is a nice plus for winter runs. Also consider wearing bright colors, a reflective vest, or even something like the Noxgear Tracer to give you good visibility on the side of the road. I have a neon pink jacket that comes out on cold dark mornings.

At the gym, be aware that the rhythm of the place will change. There will be a different group of regulars, and it may be more or less busy than you're used to. But even if everything is the same, there’s something luxurious about being able to take your time, when normally you have to squeeze your last few exercises together and rush to work. Savor that extra hour.

#3671. Xbox Wants To Be More Profitable Than PlayStation And Nintendo By 2030

Xbox CEO Asha Sharma has an ambitious goal: not only to make Xbox more lucrative, but to surpass the profit margins of its biggest gaming rivals, Sony and Nintendo.

Speaking to CNBC, Sharma said Microsoft was working to achieve this goal by mid-2030 and had a variety of plans in place, from focusing on more exclusive titles to gaining more ground in the casual games market. "We will build long-term plans for our biggest franchises across film, television, consumer products, sponsorship, live experiences, and form new partnerships globally, including China," Sharma wrote in an Xbox memo, adding that the company will invest heavily in Minecraft and that revenue growth is expected to speed up in the 2028 and 2029 fiscal years.

"By Financial Year 2030, our ambition is to be halfway to our long-term daily-player goal with sustained double-digit growth in players and engagement and industry-leading margins," she wrote.

While Sharma aims to increase Xbox's player and revenue growth in the fiscal year ending June 2027, things don't look too good for the division right now. According to Circana tracking data, US Xbox Series hardware sales fell 27% year-over-year in September 2026--reaching a new all-time September low--and Sharma recently posted online that revenue had declined in the most recent financial quarter. Sharma added that "console sales remain constrained by supply," but she was vague on the specifics. At the same time, Xbox console prices rose again in August, making it more expensive than ever to buy one compared with its original launch price in November 2020.

Xbox has also gone through a brutal "reset" phase ever since Sharma took over, with over 1,600 jobs eliminated and several studios cut from the Xbox portfolio. If Microsoft wants to make Xbox more profitable than Sony and Nintendo, it could face an uphill battle, as Xbox recorded a 10% quarterly revenue decline. By comparison, CNBC reported that Sony reached a 9.9% operating margin from game and network services alone in its latest financial year, while Nintendo was close to 16% in its fiscal year.

Xbox's current strategy seems focused on more than just gaming, as the new XP division was unveiled earlier this month. Dedicated to movies, TV, and live events, it follows several recent multimedia project announcements, including the third season of the Fallout TV series, a Call of Duty movie, a Diablo animated series, and a Minecraft theme park opening in 2027.

#3670. You All Guessed Elder Scrolls 6’s Name, And Now Here’s The Game’s Setup – Report

After eight years, Xbox is reportedly preparing to reintroduce The Elder Scrolls VI to the world. And this time, the game will apparently get an official subtitle: Sentinel. According to The Verge, Bethesda could reveal the full name next month in celebration of Skyrim's 15th anniversary. That's not all, though.

The report states that Hammerfell will serve as the setting for Sentinel. It's a massive region that's southwest of Skyrim and probably best known for being playable in The Elder Scrolls Online. As for the narrative, the RPG "will be the first game about the history of the Elder Scrolls," per The Verge. That means discovering "the secrets of these mysterious ancient artifacts" in Sentinel.

It's unknown how much Bethesda will showcase, if the re-reveal does in fact happen in November. However, the report states that gameplay demonstrations are taking place, following up Xbox CEO Asha Sharma saying she saw the game in August. At that time, Sharma teased The Elder Scrolls VI's subtitle, and fans correctly figured out it's Sentinel--at least reportedly right now. She also noted that the game's "scale and grandeur are incredible."

Earlier this year, Skyrim director Todd Howard expressed that he knows his team at Bethesda needs "to get it right" with The Elder Scrolls VI. The majority of people at Bethesda Game Studios are working on the RPG currently.

As for whether The Elder Scrolls 6 could be an Xbox console exclusive, Sharma is playing coy about that possibility. What we do know is that Bethesda has a new logo.

When it comes to the list of upcoming Marvel shows, fans are set to witness the end of an era in 2027. Daredevil: Born Again is set to end next year following a three-season run. Fans have, unsurprisingly, been in their feelings since the news was confirmed, and the cast has been opening up as well. Franchise veteran Deborah Ann Woll also spoke out in the aftermath of the cancellation news. And, more recently, she got real about one way this series’ demise differs from that of its parent show.

Woll has not only played Karen on Born Again, but she famously portrayed the journalist-turned-lawyer on Netflix’s Daredevil as well. Given that personal history, Woll has become quite attached to her character and this corner of the Marvel Cinematic Universe. The fan-favorite actress recently spoke to ComicBook about her time with the franchise and reflected on the first show’s cancellation. Per Woll, the third season of that show is her favorite of the series, and that was just one reason why the cancellation initial stung:

I mean, I think the first time we were canceled, we really didn’t know it was coming, right? Like, that third season of the Netflix one is my favorite of the three. And I thought it was really a high point in the series, and we fully expected to come back and do more. So I didn’t really get to say goodbye, and that felt like the rug being pulled out from under us.

Woll’s feelings are completely understandable, as Daredevil’s cancellation in 2018 was heartbreaking. At the time, the show’s unfortunate fate was in great part due to the shrinking role of the now-defunct Marvel Television (a banner now used by Marvel Studios’ TV arm). It’s sad to think about the notion of the True Blood alum both being surprised by the show’s conclusion and being unable to properly say goodbye to her colleagues. At the very least, though, with Born Again’s cancellation, Woll was afforded more closure:

This one? You know, you’re never sure, but I think we all sort of felt like this was the last one… as we were wrapping things up. And so, you know, I stole something from the set, and I hugged everybody I wanted to hug. And I will say this: having played a character over twelve years, you get to see someone go through such different stages of their life. And I really appreciated that they let the story take that change.

While I’m comforted by the notion of Woll having had an inkling regarding Born Again’s fate, it’s still hard to believe the show is coming to an end. There’s been quite a bit of mourning amongst fans in some respects, but the stars themselves are remaining upbeat. Series lead Charlie Cox shared a great perspective, as he emphasized how he and his collaborators are going out on their own terms. Fellow cast member Matthew Lillard also teased an exciting third season, and those comments may cheer up fans.

It’s true that there will be a lot to look forward to in this third and final season, from a loose adaptation of the famous storyline “"The Devil in Cell-Block D" to a reunion of The Defenders. Of course, we’ll also get to spend more time with Deborah Ann Woll’s Karen Page, who’s proven to be one of the MCU’s most dynamic characters. It’ll be a pleasure for me to watch her in the final season, and it’ll be sweeter knowing that Page was able to walk away from set after having given hugs and snagged a souvenir.

Daredevil: Born Again Season 3 is set to premiere in March 2027 and, in the meantime, fans can stream the first two seasons (along with the OG show) using a Disney+ subscription.

#3668. Karen Bass on Nithya Raman, Her Radical Past, and the Fight to Remain LA Mayor

Karen Bass was showing me her three iPhones when I visited her at Getty House, the official residence of the Los Angeles mayor, late last month. One was her personal phone, another was for government business, and the third had been hacked so many times that she wasn’t supposed to use it anymore. But Bass couldn’t bring herself to ditch the number, which she’s had for 20 years, because friends and colleagues still call it. So she kept the compromised phone around, monitoring its incessant ringing during our interview.

Bass, 73, has the warmth of a grandmother who wants to make sure you’re hydrated, and, as I discovered, the authority of a disappointed matriarch who expects you to know better. The intimidating part is that she can vacillate between those two sides of herself rather quickly.

With a disarming smile, she offered me a glass of water and invited me to meet her daughter and grandson, who live with her at Getty House.

Bass photographed at the Getty House in Los Angeles, September 2026.

But when I suggested that Bass, a lifelong progressive who has traveled to Fidel Castro’s Cuba to study alternatives to capitalism, was borrowing from the conservative playbook to portray her opponent Nithya Raman as a dangerous extremist, a different side of Bass came out. Suddenly I was sitting across from a stern political veteran who had little patience for people challenging her judgment.

“That’s not true,” she shot back defensively.

I mentioned a campaign email that I thought implied Raman might be antisemetic. Bass and an aide disputed my characterization, insisting that the campaign has simply criticized Raman for skipping a Jewish heritage event at City Hall.

Did she believe Raman was antisemetic? “I don’t know what she is,” Bass replied. “It depends on the time of day and day of the week.”

At one point when I asked whether she would warn her successor about the city’s dysfunctional homelessness bureaucracy, Bass took another swipe at Raman.

“Well, if she’s my successor, no, she knows it all,” Bass said with a sarcastic undertone.

Just four years ago Bass was embraced by the local progressive movement in LA. But now she’s getting flak from both sides of the political spectrum and finds herself courting conservative voters to defeat Raman, who is running to the left of Bass.

For over a year, wealthy donors have been trying to find her replacement. Rick Caruso, the billionaire developer who spent more than $100 million trying to defeat Bass in 2022, says he was encouraged by Ari Emanuel and former Governor Jerry Brown to consider another run for elected office. Spencer Pratt, the reality television villain whose house burned down in the Palisades fire, transformed his personal tragedy into an insurgent mayoral campaign, attracting wealthy Hollywood supporters and massive amounts of attention on social media that was driven by his atypical political ads and AI-generated promotional videos made by his supporters.

But neither man became Bass’s 2026 general-election opponent. Instead, the challenge came from the left, in the form of Raman, a Harvard-educated democratic socialist who even endorsed the mayor’s reelection before entering the race. Now Bass finds herself vying for Pratt supporters on the right. She’s made public safety—an issue Pratt harped on—central to her reelection campaign, and has tried to paint Raman as soft on crime. Raman is also making a play for Pratt supporters, even invoking Ronald Reagan at the beginning of the only televised debate between the two candidates since June’s primary.

Bass is even showing up with Caruso on the campaign trail now. The two appeared together this month at the developer’s luxury shopping mall in the Pacific Palisades in what amounted to an unlikely reunion given Caruso’s unflattering assessment of her leadership. “People feel let down by the city,” he told me in August. Caruso also argued that LA mayors have more power than they care to admit. “They do have enough power and they don’t use it right,” he said. But perhaps Caruso sees Bass as a more palatable option than Raman, who carries the weight of a DSA association. Caruso called the socialist organization’s platform “dangerous” and said he would be voting for Bass in the upcoming election.

Karen Bass and Rick Caruso talk while on a tour of his shopping center, Palisades Village, in the Pacific Palisades, October 20, 2026.

A September UC Berkeley Institute of Governmental Studies poll conducted for the Los Angeles Times found Raman leading Bass 39% to 28% among likely voters, with another 33% undecided. Nearly two thirds of respondents viewed Bass unfavorably. The numbers were hardly conclusive (no polls are these days), but they laid bare the fact that a politician who entered City Hall with considerable goodwill is now facing a difficult fight for another term. Bass could very well become the first Los Angeles mayor in 21 years not to be given a second term. If she wins, it’ll likely be because a lot of Pratt primary voters decided she was the lesser of two evils.

It’s a bit of an ironic situation that Bass finds herself in. Before she was mayor, before she was a congresswoman, before she became Speaker of the California state assembly, she was a teenage radical who considered running for public office an act of ideological surrender.

“Running for office was selling out,” she recalled when we spoke at a Croatian community center in San Pedro.

Has she changed? Or, like Reagan before her, has the increasingly left-leaning Democratic Party left her behind?

Bass was 14 when she signed her mother up to serve as a precinct captain for Robert F. Kennedy’s presidential campaign, she tells me. Her mother didn’t actually do the work. Bass did, riding her bicycle to campaign headquarters and immersing herself in the senator’s bid for the White House.

She was supposed to attend Kennedy’s primary-victory celebration at the Ambassador Hotel in June 1968, but her parents wouldn’t let her go because it was a school night.

“So I listened to the assassination on the radio,” she says.

The murder was devastating to Bass and her parents. Just two months earlier, Martin Luther King Jr. had been assassinated and, to Bass’s parents, it seemed like anyone involved in progressive politics would suffer the same fate.

“I was like, ‘It’s over.’ I was done,” she says. “I became much more interested in antiestablishment work.”

Her parents were reluctant to let her dive into politics. But the young Bass had already been politicized. Growing up in Los Angeles, she encountered the contradictions of establishment liberal politics. She attended Hamilton High School, which she says was predominantly Jewish, with roughly 300 Black students among its 3,000 pupils, and witnessed white flight as Black families moved into previously segregated neighborhoods.

Bass surrounded by supporters during a press conference to kick off the next phase of her reelection campaign in Los Angeles, June 9, 2026.

“It was painful,” she said. “Very confusing for a child because, you know, I’m talking Martin Luther King and all this stuff, and they’re like, ‘Oh no, not here.’”

She went on to become deeply involved in the anti-apartheid movement and learned how to organize from older activists. But by the late 1980s, she was growing increasingly frustrated with the distance between the political debates consuming her fellow activists and the violence engulfing South Central Los Angeles. The crack epidemic devastated neighborhoods, gang violence was killing young people, and elected officials only seemed to be interested in filling prisons. On the other end of the spectrum, she felt that progressive activists were more interested in relitigating the Iran-Contra scandal than they were in providing concrete relief to those suffering.

“I felt like what [progressive activists] were doing politically was theoretical and aspirational, but people were dying,” Bass says.

She quit her secure job teaching nursing at USC and founded the Community Coalition, an organization devoted to confronting addiction, violence, and poverty.

Her career change pissed off a lot of her compatriots. Bass was entering the nonprofit world, where she would have to negotiate with government agencies and accept money from the very institutions she had spent years protesting.

“I did the ultimate sellout move,” she jokes. “I took federal funding to start the organization.”

“I wanted to make a difference in people’s lives,” she says, “and my trajectory since then has been pragmatic, which has gotten me on the outs of some folks on the left. But that’s okay. As long as I’m delivering for poor people, I’m okay.”

Homelessness was Bass’s first priority when she was elected mayor. She left a secure seat in Congress to run for mayor in 2022, promising to confront the crisis with the urgency of a community organizer. It wasn’t hard to sell that vision to voters. She had experience tackling the crisis from her time at the Community Coalition.

Her signature program, Inside Safe, was designed to move people out of encampments and into temporary housing, where they could receive services and eventually secure permanent homes. For Bass, the program is evidence that her administration has made progress on an issue that befuddled her predecessors.

But the numbers tell a more complicated story. Street homelessness has declined over the course of her administration, but the city’s unsheltered population increased nearly 8% in the most recent annual count. In Raman’s council district, meanwhile, street homelessness fell roughly 49% during the same year.

Mayor Karen Bass during a debate with City Councilmember Nithya Raman with moderators from NBC4 and Telemundo 52, October 13, 2026.

Bass claims that the deeper problem is a fragmented homelessness bureaucracy. Under the current system, the city, county, and Los Angeles Homeless Services Authority share responsibilities, making it difficult to track spending and hold anyone accountable.

She wants to give the city greater authority over its own homelessness programs. But one might ask why she wasn’t able to give the city more power to fight the problem during her first term? She says her time was monopolized by moving people off the streets, and that she couldn’t simultaneously overhaul the bureaucratic inefficiencies at the homelessness agencies.

“I had to build the plane and fly it,” she tells me.

When I asked her to grade her performance on homelessness, she gave herself a B-plus. It was a confident assessment for a mayor whose signature issue became one of her most glaring political vulnerabilities during the primary. Pratt flooded the internet with videos and pictures portraying a homelessness crisis that was out of control. Whether it’s true or not that the problem got worse under Bass’s leadership was irrelevant. Pratt convinced large swaths of the city that it had.

Nothing has damaged Bass’s political standing more than the January 2025 wildfires.

When the Palisades fire erupted, the mayor was in Ghana as part of a presidential delegation. By the time she returned, the disaster had become a defining crisis of her administration.

The fire killed 12 people and destroyed thousands of homes. It also transformed the city’s politics, elevating figures such as Pratt, who lost his home and made the government’s response central to his mayoral campaign.

Bass has acknowledged that leaving Los Angeles was a mistake.

“My biggest regret was not being here,” she told me.

Bass maintains that the emergency notifications she would ordinarily have expected from public safety officials did not reach her before she left for Africa. But in the week leading up to the fires, weather forecasters were warning that the city could experience an extreme fire event. Companies were telling their employees to be safe. And news organizations were already planning how to cover the potential fires.

Bass knows that the mayor bears ultimate political responsibility, but she resists the idea that every institutional failure can be reduced to her negligence.

“Any time I made any attempts to explain, it was viewed as I was giving excuses and pointing fingers,” she says.

And yet Bass says she understands the anger of fire survivors.

“I understood and understand people’s anger because when you grieve, it is helpful if there’s somewhere that you could say, ‘This wouldn’t have happened except for that.’”

Bass is deeply familiar with the anger that comes with grief.

In 2006 her daughter Emilia and son-in-law Michael Wright were killed in a car accident. Bass told me about the painful impulse she felt to imagine how things might have turned out differently. For some time she wondered if she could have prevented their deaths.

“That was the absolute positively worst thing that could ever happen to me,” she says. “So consequently, everything since then, I feel like the worst has already happened. Nothing else could happen worse to me. Nothing.”

At Getty House, Bass tells me that she’s not going to read the state report on last year’s wildfires until it’s released to the public. She’s been accused of meddling in the LA Fire Department’s after-action report, published in October of last year, and she explained that she doesn’t want to be accused again of influencing or watering down the findings. For what it’s worth, she also said she hasn’t read the fire department’s report either.

“I have not seen it, and you know what? I don’t want to see it,” she says of a preview of the state report.

Bass’s relationship with Hollywood has soured a bit since she first took office. Meanwhile, it appears that much of the city’s creative class is siding with Raman, whose husband is an accomplished television writer who worked on 30 Rock and Modern Family.

Bass pushed for a settlement between state attorneys general and Paramount Skydance over an antitrust lawsuit that threatened to derail the company’s acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery after Paramount Skydance chief David Ellison indicated that he would move Paramount’s operations out of Los Angeles. She insists she wasn’t asking the AGs to approve the transaction. She says she just wanted to end the uncertainty hanging over the entertainment industry, which was already struggling to prevent runaway productions.

Bass says she spoke with Ellison while the lawsuit was active. She told me she was dissatisfied with the assurances he offered about preserving jobs over the next five years. But she worried that prolonged regulatory uncertainty would only compound the industry’s troubles.

The distinction mattered to Bass: She wasn’t necessarily taking the billionaire’s side, she argued. She was trying to protect the workers whose livelihoods depended on the outcome.

Bass’s budget management has also been a hot topic during campaign season, particularly the raises she negotiated for Los Angeles Police Department officers.

“She gave the police more money than they asked for, and then we had a $1 billion budget deficit [at the end of the 2024-2025 fiscal year],” says comedian and Raman supporter Adam Conover.

When Raman attacked her on this issue during the debate, Bass responded by saying her opponent was being disingenuous. “You know that some of these [fiscal management] problems have taken place over many decades,” Bass snapped back. “Frankly, it’s dishonest.”

Bass, then a Congresswoman, at a rally with then-mayor Antonio Villaraigosa in Los Angeles, California, March 23, 2011.

Then there is the downtown convention center.

The city is undertaking an approximately $2.6 billion expansion project intended to attract conferences and revive economic activity downtown.

Jason Oppenheim, the luxury real estate broker and Selling Sunset personality, sees the convention center project as an effort by the Bass administration to satisfy the unions—a very influential constituency in this city.

Oppenheim is hardly a natural ally of the DSA, but he has found himself increasingly intrigued by Raman.

“She strikes me as pragmatic and willing to go against her political base when necessary,” he tells me. “But I think a lot of people are more scared of the DSA than they are frustrated with Karen Bass’s tenure,” he says.

Oppenheim was getting a manicure when we spoke. He had not settled on a candidate yet, but he seemed at peace with the possibility of taking a political gamble.

“I don’t take risks on my nails,” he said. “I will on the mayor, but not on my manicures.”

The mayor wakes up between four and five in the morning and reads the Los Angeles Times, The New York Times, and international news outlets. The teenage activist who followed liberation movements around the world still has a fascination with foreign policy. She tells me she’s not too big a fan of her local paper these days because of how much ink it’s spilled criticizing her administration.

Bass spoke with unhoused people at an encampment during an Inside Safe operation in Los Angeles, September 26, 2024.

The mayor regularly attends Black churches, especially during campaign season. At a Pratt campaign event in South Central LA held in May, two women sitting in lawn chairs told me they were likely voting for Bass because she had recently attended their church for a Sunday service. Two more women at a community trash cleanup in the same neighborhood this October told me they were also voting for Bass because of her relationship to the neighborhood and its faith institutions.

When she was 14, Bass believed the system had failed. At 73, she believes the system can work if someone with sufficient experience and determination is running it.

Bass is not particularly impressed by the younger generation of progressive activists in Los Angeles.

“I don’t feel like there’s a real appreciation or thirst for history of past movements to learn past lessons,” she said.

She sees the Democratic Socialists of America as having the arguments that consumed earlier generations, particularly over whether ideological compromise is a betrayal or a necessary condition of achieving anything.

“At this point I stand for getting stuff done,” she told me. “I’ve always been a progressive, always supported social justice. That is a through line in my life from childhood to now.”

Bass also has a theory about what happens to young radicals as they get older. They have children and parenthood tempers their ideological purity with the practical demands of raising a family. The activists who once demanded radical change begin worrying about their children’s safety, their schools, and whether the neighborhood is a decent place to grow up. Their priorities change.

Of course Bass doesn’t see her own evolution as a retreat from her youthful convictions. She says the goals remain the same. But these days she’s working from within the system to achieve them.

The hard part for Bass will be convincing the voters who believe the system has failed them to choose her. And it leaves Bass in an uncomfortable position for a former radical: she’s defending the virtues of experience against a younger, more ideological candidate who believes Los Angeles needs something different.

Bass knows she might not get another four years to implement her policies. Even her staffers seem genuinely unsure of how election day will play out.

“Losing an election would be devastating,” she told me.

It felt like a big admission from a politician who usually projects confidence. However, Bass has endured worse than political defeat.

“There is no comparison of a parent losing a child to losing an election.”

#3667. WoW: Forever Controller Support Is A First Step To Playing The MMO On “Whatever You Want”

World of Warcraft: Forever will launch with full controller support, a first for the various versions of Blizzard's longrunning PC-exclusive MMORPG. According to Blizzard, the option to play on controller is the "first leg of a journey" to make WoW playable "on whatever you want." 

Speaking to GamesRadar, WoW executive producer and vice president Holly Longdale said Blizzard's goal is to eventually have WoW playable "wherever you want, and, at some point, on whatever you want."

The first step on that road, however, is ensuring controller support works really well. Blizzard is using the launch of Forever on November 4, the latest version of its MMO that reimagines the game's classic world and gameplay with new content and features, as a starting point.

"Looking at where things are going when we hear about Project Helix [the codename for Xbox's next console], et cetera, I think platforms will be a bit more ubiquitous," Longdale said. 

She continued: "I think just doing some of the work we're doing on gamepad [support] is going to give players a lot of flexibility that I think goes beyond consoles."

Having gone hands-on with Forever's controller support during BlizzCon 2026, I can say it works surprisingly well for a game that has been played almost exclusively with mouse and keyboard for 22 years. While modern WoW has added some barebones controller options in recent years, Forever's implementation is far superior, working seamlessly without the need for player-made addons like ConsolePort to make it usable. 

You have a surprisingly number of keybinds available at your fingertips (28, to be exact), making combat and interacting with quest NPCs a breeze. Inventory management and navigating menus is a little more cumbersome, but it does feel like a decent tradeoff for being able to play on a controller or a handheld, like the Xbox ROG Ally X. 

When WoW might be playable on something other than a PC remains to be seen, though Blizzard has made clear that if it were making a console version, it wouldn't exactly be a secret. 

But that doesn't mean WoW on consoles is still years away. Xbox's next console, Project Helix, is rumored to be a hybrid device capable of playing console and PC games, meaning WoW would likely be playable on it. According to a recent report, Project Helix is aiming for a 2028 release, may include a handheld component, and could possibly cost between $1,200 and $1,800 if Microsoft doesn't subsidize it.

In the meantime, Blizzard is plenty busy getting ready for Forever's launch, including reworking racial abilities and making improvements to the game's divisive layering system. If you bought the MMO's new optional playable race, the Skyborne, you can technically make your WoW: Forever character right now ahead of launch day. WoW: Forever launches November 4.

#3666. How to Prepare Now so the End of Daylight Saving Time Is Less Jarring

Sadly, we did not manage to abolish Daylight Saving time changes during that brief, hopeful moment a few years back, so in just a few weeks we will all be going ahead with our usual ritual: Wake up early, forgetting that the time changed during the night, then get confused when the time on our phone doesn’t match the one on the microwave. Here’s how to be a little more prepared.

Daylight saving time is what we call the time in summer, and yes, it’s daylight “saving” time, singular. This time actually gets its own time zone abbreviation: EDT (Eastern Daylight Time) instead of EST (Eastern Standard Time) on the east coast, with corresponding CDT, MDT, and PDT across the country. So in November we change from daylight time to standard time.

Specifically, daylight saving time ends at 2 a.m. on Sunday, Nov. 1, 2026. That’s when the clocks “fall back.” (In the spring, they "spring forward"—get it?) If you’re changing your clocks manually, 2 a.m. becomes 1 a.m. This means that if you’re used to waking up at 7 a.m., you’ll open your eyes after sleeping the usual amount of time to find that it is now 6 a.m.

The fall time change is a great moment for me, a night owl. When I was younger I would be thrilled to stay up an extra hour and still not feel excessively tired in the morning. These days, I’m more likely to use the time change as an assist to my morning routine. I’ll be up at 6:30 (for example) instead of 7:30, and I can get in an early workout or do some journaling.

If you’re more of a morning person, this may be a bit less pleasant. You’re going to fall asleep watching TV in the evening—earlier than you usually do, anyway. Maybe you should try to stay up a bit, to get a head start on shifting your routine an hour later.

For the creatures in your house who are blissfully ignorant of the concept of standardized time, routines are about to get a little weird. Most importantly: They’ll get hungry (and everything else) an hour earlier than usual.

If you think ahead, you can start moving breakfast time later, before the time change arrives. Instead of feeding your dog at 7, start feeding him at 7:15 now, and you’ll be less likely to get a cold nose in the face at 6 a.m. (Since we have about two weeks from this writing, you can shift the time to 7:30 after a few days, and then 7:45. You get the idea.)

Same goes for kids: Expect them to wake up an hour before the clock says they should, and to get tired (and overtired) an hour earlier than they normally would. A gradual shifting of routines will help here as well, and you may want to explain the situation ahead of time to kids who are old enough to understand. And if you expect your own tummy to be grumbling on cue? Consider a gradual change in mealtimes for yourself, as well, or at least have a snack on hand in case you need it.

When daylight saving time ends, we stop “saving” that extra hour of sunlight in the evening. Your evening workout or your evening commute will be darker and colder than before. On the bright side, we’ll see light earlier in the morning, which can be a good excuse to take a morning walk you might not otherwise take. (Morning light and morning exercise both help to set your body clock and may put you in a better mood for the day to come.)

If you head outside for exercise in the evening, check out our guide to how to layer for an outdoor run, depending on the temperature. You may also want to bring a flashlight or wear a headlamp. Here's the one I use.

It may be easier to wake up after the time change, but the flip side is that it may be harder to go to bed. This is a good time to take a look at your bedtime routine, or even to create a bedtime routine if you haven’t really had one.

I have a guide to good sleep hygiene here, but one of the most important tips is to give yourself a wind-down time in the evening—30 minutes minimum—where the lights are dim and you aren’t staring at a screen. It’s a good time to take a bath, read a book, or do something else you find relaxing. Soon you’ll be locked in to your new schedule—at least until our next time change in the spring.

#3665. Dan Campbell Addresses Jack Campbell's Possible Neck Injury After Awful Scene

Detroit Lions head coach Dan Campbell is addressing his all-pro player Jack Campbell’s potential neck injury after the star linebacker suffered what appeared to be a very serious injury during the team’s Sunday, November 1, win over the Minnesota Vikings.

“Let me start with this: You know, thoughts and prayers are with Jack and his family,” Dan, 50, told reporters during a post-game press conference on Sunday. “He’s being taken care of — we don’t have any new information. We’ll keep you updated as this goes, um, but we’re thinking of him.”

Jack, 26, was “immobilized” following what appeared to be a relatively normal tackle against Vikings tight end T.J. Hockenson on Sunday. After the Lions’ athletic training staff swarmed the linebacker, who did not appear to be able to move after his initial fall, the athlete was carefully moved onto a backboard and carted off the field.

Shortly after the hit, the Lions’ official X account shared an update on the linebacker’s status.

“Jack Campbell is being transported to a local hospital to be evaluated for a neck injury,” the post, shared via X on Sunday, read.

Several Vikings and the Lions players were seen taking a knee immediately after the hit and for the duration of Jack’s time on the field, as an audible hush fell over the crowd at Ford Field in Detroit, Michigan.

Many of the linebacker’s teammates were visibly upset after the play and while Jack was tended to on the field by medical staff. Several players were seen wiping tears from their eyes as they tried to rally their fellow teammates after the linebacker was removed from the field.

Erin Andrews spoke candidly from the sideline shortly after Jack was carted off the field, sharing what one member of the team said the defensive player means to the organization.

“He said, ‘This is Jack Campbell’s defense. I don’t hesitate to say that it goes through him and everyone in that locker room knows that,” Andrews, 48, said, sounding emotional at times. “Point blank period.”

Tom Brady, a former NFL quarterback and now FOX News color commentator, was asked how teammates return to the field and the task at hand after watching what was clearly a severe injury befall a friend. (Brody, 49, was calling the game at the time of the incident.)

“It’s very difficult for everybody, obviously, but it’s also part of what you’ve been doing your whole life,” Brady said on-air after Jack was carted off the field and play resumed. “He’s under great medical care and attention and you have to go back out there and do your job.”

The Lions ultimately handed the Vikings their first defeat of the 2026-2027 NFL season with a 19-15 win.

#3664. Ubisoft Is Pumping The Brakes On Assassin’s Creed Remakes For Now

What's next for the Assassin's Creed franchise? Following the successful launch of Assassin's Creed Black Flag Resynced earlier this--which sold very well--you'd imagine that Ubisoft would be looking to fast-track another remake while it continues work on future titles. That's not the case, as Ubisoft dropped a new update on all things Assassin's Creed, including confirmation that it's not currently working on any remakes.

"One thing we want to be transparent about today is that we currently have no other Assassin's Creed remake actively in development," Ubisoft wrote. "Our teams are already focused on the next chapter of Assassin's Creed titles, including projects you haven't heard about yet, featuring new settings and stories."

While you shouldn't expect another Assassin's Creed remake anytime soon, Ubisoft added that it will still keep "exploring opportunities" to bring older titles back. As for future projects, Ubisoft said that it's making "good progress" on its darker Assassin's Creed experience, Codename Hexe. An update on it will arrive in 2027, and Ubisoft added that the team remains focused on delivering a "unique vision" at the heart of this project. The other in-development title, Codename Invictus, is also taking shape behind the scenes. This will be a multiplayer Assassin's Creed game, and Ubisoft says hundreds of players recently got to go hands-on with an early prototype.

"One piece of feedback came through clearly though: Players saw great potential in the foundations but wanted more of the pillars that define Assassin's Creed. The team spent the past months acting on it, and Invictus is now evolving in an exciting direction that better reflects those pillars while staying true to its multiplayer ambitions," Ubisoft wrote.

For current games, Black Flag Resynced players can download one final major update. This adds New Game Plus, Nightmare Mode, new rewards, finishers, trinkets, and additional customization options to the Black Flag remake. Assassin's Creed Valhalla players aren't being left out in the cold either, as New Game Plus is being added to the Viking saga on November 5. A heavily requested feature for this particular Assassin's Creed game, the update will also add an optional progression mode where Gear, Runes, and Masteries all contribute to Eivor's overall power ranking. Players can also earn new gear and a Master Assassin outfit inspired by Naoe's look in Assassin's Creed Shadows; a new Mithril resource is being added, and you can upgrade your gear to a new "Divine" level.

While the news is good for Assassin's Creed fans, it comes amid restructuring at Ubisoft that has led to several canceled games, shut-down studios, and layoffs. Trials developer RedLynx is on the chopping block, while 72 people from Ubisoft Singapore--the studio behind Skull & Bones--were recently laid off.

U.S. President Donald Trump recently hosted several celebrities at the White House for dinner, with one of those guests being Bill Maher. Sometime later, POTUS took to social media and chastised Maher, who has joked about Trump on air on multiple ocassions. In the aftermath, Maher addressed the situation on the latest episode of his talk show (which is streamable with an HBO Max subscription). With that, the comedian dropped a joke relating to Kelly Clarkson.

Last weekend, President Trump shared his thoughts on Maher (and more topics) to Truth Social, and the post ended up including a total of 1,318 words. In the lengthy post, Trump refers to Maher as a “COMPLETE AND TOTAL LOSER” with “a Low Rated Show on equally Low Rated HBO” and capitalized those specific words as well. The President’s post came days after remarks Maher shared on Real Time days prior. The comic joked about Trump’s supposed focus on “men’s bodies” and mused that he himself was not complimented during dinner.

Amid the latest installment of Real Time – which aired on October 30th amid the 2026 TV schedule – Maher touched on several topics before shifting his focus to Trump’s viral post. The political humorist didn’t mince words when describing the aftermath of the post, and he not only name-dropped Clarkson but a certain pop star as well:

He went off on me like Kelly Clarkson in a toy store. I mean, eating with Trump is like dating Taylor Swift. It’s a lot of laughs at the time, but later on, they’re tearing you a new asshole.

The Major CBS News Claims Bari Weiss Apparently Shared With Bill Maher: ‘I Was Curious’

Bill Maher’s Taylor Swift comment seemingly references how the singer’s exes remain topics of discussion on social media even after they’ve dated. The Clarkson sentiment, however, refers to a situation that’s a bit more recent. Back in October, Clarkson posted about a negative experience she reportedly had at Art of Play, a novelty store located in Brooklyn. The singer claimed she was treated like Julia Roberts’ character from Pretty Woman when she attempted to buy a singing bird automaton.

However, the store’s management team – headed up by owner Adam Rubin – later claimed the bird was not for sale and was used for in-store events. However, Clarkson later responded to the claim by sharing a photo of the bird with a $15,000 price tag on it. Leaked security footage later revealed that Clarkson had a heated exchange with store employees. As it stands, Rubin and co. have been receiving hate on social media and have reportedly been seeking to reach out to Clarkson.

As of this writing, Kelly Clarkson has reportedly yet to touch base with the crew at Art of Play. On that note, Donald Trump has yet to respond to Maher’s latest comments regarding his post and their dinner at the White House. Whether he’ll choose to do so remains to be seen.

In the meantime, viewers can check out Real Time with Bill Maher, which airs on Fridays at 10 p.m. ET on HBO, and episodes can also be streamed later on HBO Max.

#3660. Artist With Music In GTA 6 Had No Idea About Any Of That

Cliff Richard is among the numerous famous artists who are lending their music to Rockstar's GTA 6, with Richard's classic tune "Devil Woman" appearing in the Netflix Extended Look. Richard, 86, didn't know about any of that, however, or that GTA 6 is a game and not a TV show.

Speaking to The Times (via Dexerto), Richard said of the partnership with Rockstar for GTA 6: "I was told this happened!" He said his nephew's sons told him about it. "They didn't realize I could sing like that," he said.

Richard was eventually made aware of GTA 6, but the singer doesn't know what that is. “The show is a game show, isn’t it, really? One of the biggest on TV?” he asked.

"Devil Woman" was originally released in 1976, so it's now 50 years old. Richard said he's pretty jazzed about the fact that young people will hear his music.

“People will no longer just say, ‘Oh, Cliff Richard is from the past,’” he said. “Because I am, but that past is what makes everything what it is today."

It was reported that Spotify streams of "Devil Woman" surged massively following the Netflix Extended Look in August.

For more on the music of GTA 6, be sure to check out GameSpot's rundown of all the songs in the game. The game's official score by Justice is releasing on December 11, and it will be available to stream and buy on physical media. The same cannot be said for the game itself, which is a digital exclusive. The game will be sold at retailers, but there is no disc: just a code in a box.

GTA 6 launches on November 19 for PS5 and Xbox Series X|S, and the game's file size is gargantuan.

#3657. These Sennheiser Wireless Headphones Are 32% Off Right Now

In a market where every year there is an expectation of releasing a new model, how long tech companies take to feel the need to upgrade a product is a testament to how good the product is. The Sennheiser Momentum 4 has been around since 2022, and they were only succeeded this summer with the Sennheiser Momentum 5. However, they are still great headphones, and with their $204.60 price (originally $299.99) after a 32% discount, they're a great opportunity to get top-quality headphones at a more than reasonable price.

The Momentum 4 competes with other flagships from its time, including the Sony 1000XM5 and the Bose QuietComfort 45, in terms of comfort, design, audio quality, and other features. The Momentum 4 has a more bass-forward sound compared to its competition, but it's still balanced. The biggest con is that you don't have full EQ control, only being able to select certain presets from the Momentum app. The ANC is great, but not a match compared to the Sony and Bose competition. Where it does beat its competition is with the codecs it supports, including AAC, AptX, AptX Adaptive, and SBC codecs. This means better audio quality for Android devices than the Sony or Bose options.

The battery is powerful, reaching about 60 hours of juice at mid-level. It also has a 3.5mm audio cable, so you can use it wired. The microphone is perfect for making calls, with four-MEMS-mics helping make your voice stand out even in noisy environments. You can see more features from the Momentum 4 in PCMag's "excellent" review. If you're looking for a bargain on an established flagship headphone model without having to pay the premium in 2026, the Sennheiser Momentum 4 are a great pair to consider.

#3656. WoW: Forever Won’t Have Dead Servers

World of Warcraft: Forever will avoid repeating WoW Classic's mistakes and will have tools to prevent "dead" or "unsustainable" server rulesets, Blizzard said.

In the past, various WoW Classic servers became "dead" over time, as players either stopped playing or transferred to other servers. Those massive drops in population had major ramifications for players left on the server being unable to find groups for raids or dungeons, as well as for the server's economy and auction house. In some extreme cases, Blizzard gave away free character transfers so players could leave their "dead" servers behind.

While Forever is going a different route with what are essentially mega servers tailored around specific rulesets, some players might still have anxiety when it comes to picking a ruleset that will be a healthy place to play long-term. 

In the latest episode of the WoW: Forever podcast, Blizzard said it has tools it can use if a ruleset's population becomes "unsustainable." Senior game designer Josh Greenfield gave the example of Forever's separate RP and (newly added) RP-PvP server rulesets. He said there were initially concerns about splitting up the RP community, fearing that one or both of the rulesets wouldn't be able to stand the test of time. He said Blizzard now believes "it will be fine," but does have options should the worst happen. 

"If someday down the line, if something happens and one or both of those populations can't quite sustain themselves, we have options if we do need to say link up their auction houses or allow them to group for instanced content," Greenfield said.

Greenfield said it's not something Blizzard will jump to unless absolutely necessary and that it's committed to its current separate-ruleset path. Blizzard debated the idea of rulesets during Forever's development and discussed letting players from different rulesets group together for instanced content or combining auction houses.

However, it landed on wanting to maintain distinct communities, in part because of the differences in server economies when it comes to PvE and PvP rulesets, with Greenfield using an example of how it's easier to farm for gold and items on a PvE server. That in turn opened up debates on whether these cross-ruleset players would be able to trade items with one another and the need for other restrictions.

"Ultimately, these are different mindsets, these are different rulesets," Greenfield said the team decided. "Let's keep them separate for now. That is a part of original WoW that we don't want to just throw out completely. But I think the tech is set up in such a way that if we ever did really feel like we needed to make a change, we could do so."

He said those options are merely "levers we can pull if we need to" and that it's important for Blizzard to "stay flexible." That's good news, and will likely give players worried about choosing the wrong ruleset some relief. 

Blizzard is keeping busy in the handful of days left before Forever's launch. It previously detailed how it's making improvements to Forever's divisive layering system in time for release, and announced major changes to racial abilities. 

In a first for WoW, Forever will be fully playable on a controller. WoW executive producer and vice president Holly Longdale recently said Forever's controller support is a step towards WoW being playable "wherever you want" and "on whatever you want."

WoW: Forever arrives November 4. If you want to be ready for launch day, you can technically make up to three WoW: Forever characters right now.

#3655. Heidi Klum Teases Her Latest Halloween Costume

Halloween is just around the corner—and what does that mean? It means that Heidi Klum, the undisputed queen of the scariest night of the year, will soon reveal her incredible new costume. After dressing up as an anthropomorphic worm, an incredibly realistic ET, and a chimpanzee complete with prosthetic facial features and ears, the supermodel is ready to amaze us once again.

Back in September, she revealed to People that she was already hard at work planning her next big costume. While she didn’t reveal any details—which is perfectly understandable—she did hint that it would be a “very, very bloody” look and that it “goes very well with red wine.” She’s given a few clues; the latest one she shared on her Instagram profile.

“What’s my costume?” the supermodel asked her followers, attaching a spooky close-up of some prosthetics ready to transform her into who knows what. The image appears to include a shiny brain, a blue tube resembling a sea creature, fleshy tissue, and a yellow sac that could be a honeycomb, coral, earwax—in short, anything.

Of course, many have tried to come up with an answer. Some suggested it might be Ursula from The Little Mermaid; others noted similarities to the vanity monster portrayed by Demi Moore and Margaret Qualley in The Substance, while another user pointed out that the image resembles the appearance of the zombies in The Last of Us.

In an interview with NBC’s Hollywood ReelTime, special effects makeup artist Mike Marino—who has created some of the model’s most iconic Halloween looks—revealed that this year’s costume is the most complicated one he’s ever worked on.

It seems almost impossible for Klum to follow last year’s incredible costume; on the 25th anniversary of her famous Halloween party, she appeared as the mythological Medusa. Her body was entirely covered in green scales; she had a long tail and moving snakes instead of hair, while her husband, Tom Kaulitz, dressed as a Greek soldier turned to stone.

It’s quite the challenge to top that legendary getup. Yet we’re certain the former Victoria’s Secret Angel won’t disappoint. So mark your calendar for this weekend to find out whom Heidi Klum will be impersonating.

#3654. Patrick Stewart Dies At 86

Beloved actor Patrick Stewart has died at the age of 86. The veteran of stage and screen was best known for his many years as Star Trek's Jean-Luc Picard and X-Men's Charles Xavier, though he also had notable roles in video games, including The Elder Scrolls IV: Oblivion and Castlevania: Lords of Shadow.

"We announce with grew sorrow the passing of Sir Patrick Stewart yesterday at his home in Los Angeles, in the loving care of his beloved wife Sunny, following a brief and poignant journey with Alzheimer's Disease and Lewy Body Dimentia" a statement on his official Instagram reads. "He has been held in the warm embrace of family and friends, surrounded by live music, prayer, tears, laughter, and the kind of profound emotion that only he could inspire after a lifetime of devotion to us all. We will forever cherish the peaceful ease and reflection on his face, an enduring reminder of his invincible grace."

Stewart's role as Picard made him a household name, and following the conclusion of Star Trek: The Next Generation, he reprised the role in several Star Trek films as well as the series Star Trek: Picard.

Though best known for his live-action roles like Picard and Xavier, Stewart was also known for his iconic voice. Alongside the aforementioned games like Oblivion and Castlevania: Lords of Shadow (and its sequel), Stewart had voice roles in everything from American Dad to The Prince of Egypt. He also narrated the Ted movies, with his friend Ian McKellen taking over the role for the recent Ted series on Peacock.

#3653. Anthony Boyle Talks Sam Bankman-Fried and ‘The Altruists,’ a Tale of Sex and Crypto

Given how many venal tech billionaires have grabbed our attention over the last several years, you’d be forgiven for having only a hazy memory of Sam Bankman-Fried. He was the cryptocurrency whiz kid whose exchange, FTX, made him one of the richest men in the world, and who forged a charmingly slackerish persona: a shabbily dressed nerd with good intentions. As a believer in the effective altruism movement, SBF planned to donate his riches to charity. Instead, he is now serving a 25-year prison sentence for fraud and conspiracy.

Anthony Boyle slips under SBF’s skin in The Altruists, the new Netflix limited series chronicling the rise and fall of FTX—as well as the relationship between Bankman-Fried and Caroline Ellison (Julia Garner), his on-and-off romantic and business partner. The Belfast-born Boyle is best known to American audiences for his roles in historical dramas like House of Guinness (as 18th-century Irish lord Arthur Guinness), Say Nothing (as IRA leader Brendan Hughes), and Masters of the Air (as WW2 Air Force officer Harry Crosby). He got his break while still in college when he was cast as Scorpius Malfoy in the original cast of Harry Potter and the Cursed Child in London’s West End.

Anthony Boyle as Sam Bankman-Fried and Julia Garner as Caroline Ellison, The Altruists, 2026.

Ellison’s character would love that. The geek love she and SBF share in the series is complicated and cringe-inducing. She writes Harry Potter fanfic and considers herself polyamorous; he’s a virgin wowed by her brainy sophistication. They egg each other on, bound together by their hunger for risk and their desire to win, whatever the game and whatever the cost. Throughout it all, they remain convinced that they are the good guys.

The Altruists drops November 19, in the midst of a Hollywood tech billionaire reckoning that includes the Sam Altman biopic Artificial, Musk, the Elizabeth Holmes doc You Can See Everything, and Aaron Sorkin’s follow-up to The Social Network, The Social Reckoning. Boyle says he hasn’t seen any of those films yet, though he was originally set to play SBF in another movie that fell through. “I was sort of heartbroken,” he tells me, “because I’d spent a couple of months prepping, I had turned down other projects, and then it was taken away from me. I was like, I’m never gonna be able to do that voice that I worked so hard on!”

Yet when his agent called with news of the Netflix project, Boyle was hesitant. “My heart was already broken by [SBF] once,” he says. But the scripts for The Altruist—written by Graham Moore, the screenwriter of The Imitation Game—changed his mind. “It’s so funny and more about the relationship between him and Caroline,” the actor says now, “about their love story and them goading each other to do all this.”

During his initial meeting with Moore, Boyle stayed in character as Bankman-Fried. “I

was complaining about getting off of a Zoom with Mark Zuckerberg, because that’s the tone of the show. It can be quite irreverent at some points, and then other scenes are kind of heartbreaking.” It won him the part. “Thankfully,” he says, “all my prep didn’t go to waste!”

Vanity Fair: It’s funny that you were so eager to live in Sam Bankman-Fried’s head. He is such an anxious figure.

Boyle: There’s a lot of anxiety in him. You can even tell in his speech patterns: He corrects himself and goes back and forth, like his internal metronome is going so quickly at all times. He’s like a hummingbird, like his heart’s beating so quick. But thankfully I didn’t take any of that home with me.

Anthony Boyle as Sam Bankman-Fried, The Altruists, 2026.

At a couple of points in the series, he says, “I know I’m not a normal person.” There’s an ongoing public conversation right now about a lot of these tech moguls believing they know better than the rest of us. Did you think of SBF as someone with that kind of Superman complex?

I think the opposite. I played him as someone who was profoundly insecure. There’s this thing of broken men building empires. He has this idea of: I am FTX. So if I can make FTX the biggest, the richest, if I can have the most of something…. That’s not someone who’s comfortable in his own skin. I was interested in what possessed someone to become the world’s youngest billionaire. I’m not really interested in money or crypto or finance. It was: What makes them do the things that they do?

Sam is a nerdy guy, but as soon as he gets successful, he hangs giant posters of himself everywhere. Is he burning for the world to recognize him and admire his empire?

Do you know the poem “Ozymandias” [by Percy Bysshe Shelley]? There’s a bit in the show where I’m looking up at this great poster of myself, and it reminded me of that line: “Look on my works, ye mighty, and despair!” I asked Graham, “Can I quote that poem in the show?” And he said, “Originally called that episode ‘Ozymandias!’”

Talking about wanting to be recognized—when I was prepping for this, I went to a crypto guy’s birthday party in Los Angeles. He was paying a DJ a million dollars for one evening, but he built this plinth above the DJ decks for him and his friends so you had to look at him. A lot of these crypto people, who maybe didn’t have buzzing social lives—wallflowers who didn’t know how to communicate—became billionaires. And what this guy had done with it was to throw money at a very famous DJ, and then raise himself above him. It reminded me of the scene where Sam has a 100-foot poster behind him. It was like, Wow, this is that sort of man in his mum’s basement who just wants the world to see him.

In Sam’s case, his roaring egotism is somewhat awkward because he’s also obsessed with the idea of being altruistic. At one point in the show, a leader of the Effective Altruism movement sees this lavish party he’s thrown and says, “Uh, this isn’t very altruistic.”

Yes, he’s spent a lot of money on confetti cannons! That dichotomy is what’s really fascinating about him, because I think both of those two things are true. I think he really is altruistic, and I think he does have narcissistic tendencies.

I read that you corresponded with him in prison. What did you want to know?

Annoyingly for this interview, I promised him that I wouldn’t divulge anything. I asked him to open his heart up to me, and he really did. He was very forthcoming with over 100 questions in emails. He answered, I’d say, 98% of them. Even the ones that he didn’t answer were very telling for me, because you’re like a detective, trying to figure out how he answers them and in what way. And can you trust it?

As we see in the series, he insisted on doing interviews throughout the scandal. Even when his lawyers were telling him to stop.

When I was playing those scenes, it was like: I can outsmart this; I can get in front of it. I can just explain this to them. You know, he went to jail for stealing the money—but if he didn’t go to jail, a year later to the day, all of that money would have been back, and tenfold. He invested in Anthropic. He invested in the biggest AI companies. His argument was: Look, I know the markets. What you all see is a bird falling to certain death. What I can see is that the bird is swooping, and will come back up. I read last week that said Sam might have been the world’s first trillionaire had he not gone to jail, because all the AI companies are now flourishing.

Julia Garner as Caroline Ellison and Anthony Boyle as Sam Bankman-Fried, The Altruists, 2026.

The show frames Sam and Caroline as a love story. But it’s hard to tell if they are egging on each other’s delusions, or if this is kind of a game that’s fueling their relationship.

They’re obsessed with games. Even the first time they meet, they are playing a game. This isn’t in the show, but in my head, the scene that I sort of created for myself to understand him was: He’s playing World of Warcraft, and on the same screen he loses $100 million, and then he dies in World of Warcraft. He’s like, Fuck!, and feels more emotional about the game than about other people’s money.

It does feel like the real-life consequences are very abstract to him. Like he’s busy trying to outplay everyone and not thinking: This is going to cause somebody to go bankrupt and ruin their lives.

I think that’s the great tragedy of it, because people did go bankrupt, and people unfortunately died by suicide through this. Marriages broke up. Families tore apart because all of their money was in this. And that’s something that we have to remember when talking about the show. There were real-world consequences because of this crash.

There’s a whole spate of movie projects this fall that suggest tech bros are the new supervillains. But it sounds like you didn’t approach the character that way at all.

My viewpoint on it is that Sam wants to do good. But I think the best-laid plans of mice and men often [go awry]. It’s easy to say I’m going to give away all these billions—and then suddenly you’re not in your mum’s basement, and you’re hanging out with Katy Perry, and you think, This feels pretty good to me. I don’t think people should have that amount of power.

You are Mr. Period Actor. Is this the first time that you’ve played a character living in the present?

I feel like it is. It’s the first time I had to act with a laptop and an iPhone, and it’s so annoying. There’s no one there that you’re looking at. You’re just looking at a green screen. And then it [causes problems]—like, Oh, we saw the camera in the reflection when you turned it that way. These things that I didn’t have to deal with before because I was, as you said, Mr. Period Man.

Even Say Nothing was set in the 1970s and ’80s, well before cell phones.

One of your most recent period characters is Arthur Guinness in House of Guinness, and there’s been some buzz about your full-frontal nude scene on that show. I’m just curious if there’s anything that you would not do on screen.

That’s such a funny question. I guess whatever they write in the script, I’d look at it and see if I wanted to do it, but probably not! Like when I did that scene, it was in service of the character and in service of the moment. I wanted that character to feel like he's in control of the world and that these are all peasants that are beneath him and he doesn’t care. Very opposite to Sam, who I think has a lot of body shame.

Somehow, I don’t know that the world wants to think about Sam Bankman-Fried naked.

You never know, man. There’s something out there for everyone.

This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

#3652. Don’t Expect Destiny 3 At The Game Awards, Bungie Says

Destiny's future lies in its past, as Bungie is working to bring content from the infamous Destiny vault back to the game. Big plans are in place to rework fan-favorite campaigns like the Red War and Forsaken back into Destiny 2, and while that content won't be out for quite a while, Bungie has also detailed what you should not expect from the studio as the year winds down. Long story short: Don't expect to see Destiny 3 teased at The Game Awards.

"Knowing we are early in incubating our future and actively working on projects to bridge us to that new home, don't expect us to make a Destiny announcement at the TGAs this year, or to randomly drop a logo that sets the world on fire right away," head of product Josh Deane wrote.

Bungie says it secured an "initial greenlight to begin scoping the work" back in June, and a yet-to-be-revealed studio will help with its Destiny legacy content revival. To keep fans up to date, the studio has unveiled a progress bar, with which will signal when major milestones have been reached:

"Right now, we are in our pre-production, proof-of-work stage where we will ensure the process is working and hitting our quality bar as we port the legacy content. We expect this part of the process to last until roughly January/February. From that point we expect full production will be about 12 months. to fully complete the porting process. It’s a lot of content," Deane added.

What else is on the Destiny horizon? Deane said that players can look forward to "anchor" events, like a new celebration in Destiny 2 similar to Moments of Triumph, and Destiny Legacy, which Deane described as being "the whole experience" that needs to be served to where players are today. While the wording was vague, it sounds as if Destiny 1 content might come to Destiny 2. Deane said more information will be revealed next year, and both announcements will feature a new progress bar in February. Bungie also teased a mystery third project.

Overall, Bungie says it's on track with plans to unvault Destiny 2 content, has plans to celebrate the franchise, and is "building a new future" for Destiny. At the same time, Bungie is also continuing to make big changes to its extraction shooter Marathon, which launched earlier this year. March 2027 could be make or break for the game, as it continues to build out connected PvE, PvP, and PvEvP experiences, as well as options for solo players and crews.

#3651. I Tried Strava's New Strength Coach Feature, and I'm Optimistic

Strava has built its reputation on runs, rides, and swims. Strength training, however, has always felt like an afterthought in the app. Strava is trying to close that gap with its new guided strength workouts, and I spent some time with the beginner session to see whether it delivers.

The update brings guided workouts directly in the app. Instead of just logging that you lifted, you're walked through each exercise with animations, and you track sets and reps live as you go. Tap into any exercise, and you'll find form guidance, tips, and the specific muscles it targets.

When you finish, everything (every exercise, set, and rep) is saved automatically to your activity through the Workout Log. Your muscle map then updates to show where the effort went, which is a neat way to see at a glance whether you've been neglecting certain areas.

I started with the beginner workout, and I want to be clear about who it's for: true beginners. There's no equipment required, so you don't need dumbbells, bands, or a gym membership. If you've been lifting for years, this isn't going to challenge you—but that's clearly not the point. For this first workout, it's designed to lower the barrier to entry.

The interface is clean and easy to use. I especially liked the graphics, which make it simple to follow along without having to pause and decipher what a movement is supposed to look like. Everything worked smoothly throughout, with no glitches, lag, or lost progress.

Exercise instructions sometimes cut off. A few of the written descriptions were truncated with no way to see the full text, so I couldn't always read the full guidance on form.

Switching sides isn't always clear. For movements that work one side at a time, it wasn't obvious when I was supposed to switch. A simple cue or prompt would go a long way, especially for beginners who are already juggling a lot of new information.

Strava says more workout series will arrive before the end of the year, which should give the feature more range beyond that first beginner session. The company is also planning additional ways to log strength work:

Screenshot uploads: Snap a screenshot of text-based sets and reps from a training plan or notes app and import it instantly.

Build-your-own workouts: Create custom sessions instead of relying only on Strava's.

More partner integrations: So strength data can flow in automatically from wherever you already train.

These additions are what could turn this from a nice beginner tool into something I'd actually use. The real test will be whether Strava delivers the variety, progression, and range that lifters need to stick with it over time. For now, if you're new to strength work or curious, the free sample workout is an easy way to try it out. I'll be watching to see where Strava takes it from here.

#3650. Which 'Criminal Minds' Stars Are — And Aren't — Returning After Cast Exit?

Criminal Minds is wrapped up with season 20 — but not every cast member is coming back after a shocking exit.

Criminal Minds, which premiered in 2005, follows a group of criminal profilers who work for the FBI as members of its Behavioral Analysis Unit. The crime drama explores different fictional cases and shows how behavioral analysis helps the team locate their unknown subjects.

The original Criminal Minds series was revived by Paramount+ after its initial conclusion in 2020. Criminal Minds: Evolution brought back most of the cast with Joe Mantegna, A.J. Cook, Vangsness, Aisha Tyler, Adam Rodriguez and Paget Brewster reprising their roles. Other key characters — such as Matthew Gray Gubler‘s Reid — have made cameos.

The first season of Criminal Minds: Evolution (a.k.a. season 16 of the OG Criminal Minds series) introduced Voit as the main antagonist. The BAU spent the entire season hunting down the prolific killer, who they linked to 62 murders and was the mastermind behind setting up an online network of fellow serial killers.

Voit’s status as the villain was left up in the air when he had significant memory loss that caused him to no longer be labeled as a psychopath. Gilford and the rest of the Criminal Minds cast have acknowledged that Voit can’t remain on the show for good.

“I was supposed to leave the show a while ago and I’ve been pitching, ‘Well, I have to leave at some point. If you’re not going to kill me, we should have a spinoff,'” Gilford quipped exclusively to Us in May 2025. “It’s called Criminal Mind: Voit and it follows what Voit is doing when he is out in the world. Somehow he either escapes or he gets released and he is this white whale to the BAU. So Criminal Minds can keep going and having their [unsub] of the week — but they’ll always be like, ‘I wonder if Voit had something to do with this.'”

Voit was ultimately written off ahead of season 20.

“We can both hope [my character Voit will return] but all I know is I’m not there filming right now,” he told Us in July 2026 of his potential return for season 20 of Criminal Minds: Evolution. “It was hard to say goodbye. It definitely was one of my favorite characters I’ve ever gotten to play and partially because what a gift.”

He continued: “Every season I got to do a different side of this character. It wasn’t like I was just doing the same thing every year.”

For Gilford, Criminal Minds was the perfect challenge, adding, “To give this guy some redemption and go out on a good guy note — so to speak — was nice. It’s weird. You wrap a show and a lot of times you’re like, ‘I don’t know if I’m coming back next year and if we’re going to have another season in general.’ On this, I did know that it was the end.”

Gilford told Us he struggled to say goodbye to Criminal Minds.

“It was a bummer and I am really like, ‘I’m not good with emotions,'” he shared. “So I literally — before they even officially wrapped — I had a feeling it was the last take. I just left. I didn’t say goodbye to anyone. I just snuck out. They’re like, ‘Zach, where are you? Where’d you go?’ And then a few people saw me driving out of my car. I’m like, ‘Bye, I’ll see you later.'”

Keep scrolling to see who is and isn’t coming back in season 20:

Mantegna is set to return in the role of Rossi, which he has played since taking over for Mandy Patinkin in the original Criminal Minds show.

Cook will return to play JJ, who is still mourning the loss of her husband.

Vangsness is reprising the role of Garcia.

Gilford’s serial killer character isn’t expected to return — at least during season 20.

Hatanaka’s Tyler will remain an important part of the show in season 20.

Rodriguez is returning as Luke, who has been mourning a loss.

Prentiss is alive and well in season 20 of Criminal Minds.

#3649. GTA 6’s Attention To Detail Is Getting A Little Ridiculous

Only a few more weeks remain before Grand Theft Auto 6 launches on PS5 and Xbox Series X|S, and while Rockstar Games recently lifted the lid on its big open-world sequel, that's still not enough. There's definitely value in approaching a game with as little knowledge as possible so that you can enjoy any potential surprises, but we're not those people.

Instead, senior video producer Jake Dekker decided to grab a folder of high-resolution GTA 6 screenshots--a whole 99 of them, not including the promotional images for GTA 6's Ultimate Edition--and analyzed dozens of them for hidden details. Here's what he found in the first part of his JPEG investigations.

Unsurprisingly, GTA 6 is loaded with small details, callbacks to previous games in the series, and some technical wizardry. There are frazzled beards, the subtle effects of gravity, realistic scars, and even NPCs showing what the ravages of time and a tropical climate can do to flesh, proving GTA 6's location of Leonida is packed to the gills with small touches. One of the best hidden details in these screenshots is the hard currency: Every dollar bill is printed right in the United States of Paranoia. Hey, it's legal tender in a video game!

For more GTA 6 investigations, you can check out several more videos from the team. They've analyzed how immersive the game will be, from its introduction of a fuel economy to a closer look at how actions have consequences. In other GTA 6 news, you can read about how the cops will release the hounds to catch you, how you can be a crappy person to NPCs, and how big the game's map will be (spoiler: pretty big).

Legendary rocker Cliff Richard also recently learned that some of his music is in GTA 6, and while he's not entirely clued up on the game franchise, he's still happy that his 1976 song "Devil Woman" is reaching a new audience.
